div.head: " CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL" CHAT.

I regret to learn, on authority which cannot be gainsaid, that the operation on Mr. Gladstone's eye has not had such a speedily successful result as was hoped, and indeed at one time was believed to be accompanying it. The first calculation of the medical men was that in three weeks the ex-Premier would be able to resume his studies, but much more than this time has elapsed since the operation, and I am informed there is no likelihood that he will be able to use the affected eye for some time to come. Mr. Gladstone's friends are not without hope that his stay at Pit'ochry will have a healing effect upon the eye, and the right bon. gentleman himself is understood to be in much better spirits now than at any time since his retirement from the Premiership. It is expected that an examination of the eye will take place on the right hon. gentle- man's return to Hawarden.

The great fish market of London—that Billings- gate which has become famous for giving a name to the slang of its frequenters—is beginning to feel the effects of competition. It is Corporation pro- perty, and lies beneath the shadow of the Tower of London, and within sight of the new bridge of which the city authorities are so proud. The new fish market at Shadwell has been so affecting the Billingsgate trade that the Corporation have been driven to reduce the Billingsgate toll on sea-borne fish by one-half of the amount hitherto charged. The Lonnage of fish landed at Billingsgate has not fallen off because of the rapid expansion of business at Shadwell. The Corporation have,therefore,taken action in time. The fact that the Billingsgate sup- plies have remained at the figures of the last two years, and that the Shadwell supplies have enor- mously risen,implies that a greater consumption of this article of food is going on in the metropolis or in the towns around, with which it communicates.

A rough fellow of disordered wits, who has got them still further disordered by reading of the as- sassination of the French President and the other doings of the Anarchists, created a sensation in Palace Yard on Monday afternoon by attempting to stab a lady as she was entering St. Stephen's Hall on her way into the Nouse of Commons. The luna- tic, or miscreant, who was armed with a clasped pocket knife, was fortunately. prevented from in- flicting injury by the policeman at the entrance to the hall. The knife glanced along the lady's dress, and nearly penetrated her arm. The lady is the wife of Professor Sandys, the public orator at Cam- bridge, and she was about to be shown over the building by Sir Richard Temple. The attack did not prevent her from appearing afterwards in the lobby, where she was the recipient of much sym- pathy from her friends. It caused at first some consternation, and gave rise to the usual exaggera- tion; but as the facts became known, and it was discovered to be the act of a madman, the relief was great.

The Church Army is following very closely in the footsteps of General Booth and his Salvationists. In imitation of the General's farming scheme at Hadle.igh, in Essex, for the training of men for a colonial life, the Church Army is about to take pos- session of an estate near Thetford, in Suffolk, for a similar purpose. It is to be fitted up as a farm, where steady and trustworthy young men without means will be taught farm work and then sent to Canada. The Army has an extensive emigration agency in Montreal, and as it has also various labour homes it will be able to absprb the young fellows as soon as they become ripe for genuine colonial work. Many individual units will be bene- fited by the scheme, but it will hardly touch the fringe of the labour problem.

I hear that, consequent on the decision of the Home Department to introduce into this country the Bertillon anthropometric method for the mea- surement of criminals: Dr. J. G. Garson, who for many years was Sir D. Flower's assistant at the Museum of the College of Surgeons, and is a mem- ber of the Council of the Anthropological Society, has been appointed by the Home Secretary to be superintendent for the measurement of criminals. The principal duty appertaining to the new post will be that of instructing prison warders as to the correct scientific method of measuring prisoners, so as to allow of is being brought gradually into operation ; and Dr. Garson will also be required to make periodical visits of in,pec tion to the prisons throughout the country to see that the measure- ment is effectively done. Sir M. Bradford is,l learn hopeful of the best results from the new departure.

Even St. Swithin's Day is being subjected to the test of statistics, and the world is being robbed of its superstitions one by one. William Tell ha's been taken away; •so has Robin Hood. The Thirteen Club exists and flourishes; a dead set has been made at Shakespeare himself by American sceptics; and it is possible than some unbelieving TGry, jealous of the great reputation which Mr. Glad- stone is leaving behind him, may rise up one day and,under the title of the Gladstone myth, question the very existence of the renowned Liberal leader. The only superstition that, thanks to Mr. Andrew Lang, seems to be thriving and enjoying renewed vitality, is that of the humble and vulgar ghost, who can give no very adequate account of his reasons for revisiting the glimpses of the moon, and whose chief reason for returning to the haunts of men is a mental perturbation as to the fate of hidden treasure. But as for z-t. Swithin, the statis- tics of nearly half a century show that it does not matter much whether the day is wet or dry, as rain falls on the just and the unjust with its usual indifference either to the reputation ot the saint or the convenience and comtort of the pedestrian. The heavy rains which fell on the St.Swithin's Day of this year need not disconcert even the most nervous agriculturist or excursionist. Relentless meteorological science has already begun to reckon up the rainy days and the dry days with the view of knocking one nail more into the coffin of the legend.

Old Parliamentary hands who have seen the same thing done Session after Session for many years know very well that Sir W. Harcourt does not expect to carry half of the Bills which he pretended to rescue from the general wreckage on Wednes- day. But when the House laughed over and over again at his lengthening pro,zramme the,expression of his catisfaction at the good humour of members was in Sir William's best style of .dramatic sur- prise. The fact of the Parliamentary situation is just this. The only Bills which the Government are anxious to carry are the Evicted Tenants Bill and the Scotch Local Government Bill; and if they get these through the • House, with any measures that are really uncontroversial, they will be ex- tremely well satisfied. As Wednesday's unloading is only the first instalment of the process of disem- barking the cargo, it will be followed by a further unshipping by and by; and Sir William's estimate that the House will be up by the end of August will no doubt be confirmed by the result. Notwith- standing the criticism of Mr. Balfour, and his pre- tence of believing that the programme of work un- folded on Wednesday will keep the House till the end of October or the beginning of November, there cannot be the slightest room for doubting that there is the most complete understanding between the two front benches as to the end of the Session.

As to the 317ners' Eight Hours Bill, it is quite impossible to carry it except by unduly protracting the sittings. It has been retid a second time, and has just crossed the threshold of the committee stage. But the Government, having given it sup- port, are bound to give it a chance, and it is in the peculiar position pointed out by Sir W. Harcourt of not being a party measure, but of having eager sup- porters and bitter opponents on both sides of the House, and even on the two front benches. As soon as the committee stage is resumed the antagonists of the Bill will crowd the notice paper with amend- ments to a degree that will compel the Government to admit that it is only a waste of time to attempt to pass it. Then it will be sacrificed, like the others, to the general desire for a long holiday.

Forcing Children to Eat. Much harm is often done by forcing children to take even wholesome food which they dislike. Usually it is possible to cultivate a taste for any article of diet,but it sometimes happens that children, like their elders, really cannot eat certain kinds of food,and in that case their taste should be respected. Over-rieidity about eating between meals is a mistake in the case of children who are only able to digest a little at a time. We know young mothers so strict that their children are never allowed to touch a biscuit, or a sweet, or a morsel of cake when they are taken tocall at the houses of friends, but it rarely happens that such children are stronger or more healthy than those who are allowed a little more freedom. To hear a little girl of five Dr six solemnly refuse a sweetmeat or a cream biscuit with the wistful remark, " Mother does not let me eat between meals," somehow makes one sorry both for child and parent.
Beauty Sleep

All nature teaches us that the -Creator intended us to take rest when the world is darkened. The birds, in natural obedience to His intention,hide their bright eyes under downy wings. Flowers fold their petals and nod upon their stalks, and most of the animal kingdom seek their habitatious and compose themselves to sleep. Sleep banishes the weary lines of the face. Tempor- ary oblivion is a natural part of at least one-third of each day's life, and is as necessary to a healthful exist- ence as food and drink to the body. _

The busy woman think; herself 'too much occupied to heed thc insistance of nature in regard to rest, and is punished by subsequent ill-health. Perfect health is the true foundation of all beauty. Those who have accepted this theory, and devoted a portion of their time to securing and retaining health, universally add their testimony in favour of its truth. There is not one of the so-Called complexion specialists who do not advise one to " retire as early as pos3ible." If one cannot always go to bed in time to secure the " beauty sleep," which is always befoie midnight, then the needed rest can be secured at anytime during the day when it is most convenient ; but one should always endeavour to make up for lost sleep, just as much as for lost time. " Tired nature's sweet restorer,bal my sleep," is a tonic far superior to all the mixtures prepared by the hand of man for the restoration of an exhausted system, and lack of it mars the spirit and destroys the looks.

In the young, insufficient sleep brings premature wrinkles. From seven to nine hours of sleep are neces- sary, accordiniu to different individual systems. If the system is in a normal condition it will be its own indi- cator of the amount of sleep needed to keep it in per- fect repair. As far as possible the time for retiring should be regular. Sleep inducA by narcotics is a poor sub- stitute for the sound sleep of health. It is simply an oblivion, which is excusable only when illness compels it, and even then the benefits of such sleep are almost always counterbalanced by the evil effects of the drug that procures it. Health, pride, beauty, and the moral sense are all affected, and frequently ruined, by the use of opiates, and the healthy person who makes use of them commits a crime against nature, which she punishes sooner or later. .When insomnia attacks, a physician shouli be con- sulted, for continued lots of sleep will undermine the constitutim and ruin both the looks and disposition.

To Keep the Boys Quiet. It is easy enough to keep the little girls busy, happy, and quiet at the same time; but anyone who knows boys knows also how hard it is to manage them during a con- valescence, a spell of bad weather, or the presence of an invalid. Give a girl a box of pieces, a pair of scissors, and a needle and thread, and she asks no more for hours, because brain and fingers are both employed in creating something. The creative instinct is just as strong in a boy as a girl,but for want of suitable materials and wise direction his efforts lead him into mischief, and his family and friends label him " mischievous ; can't keep his bands off a thing." The small boy who split all his mother's clothes-pins in half did not do it from a sense of mischief, but because his desire to do and make something was so strong, and ' his announcement that he had made "whole yots of close-pins," was proof nositiv.l of this fact ; nor was he _worse than the wee girlie who cut zig-zag into a yard of , new material for "patches." Both wanted to "help mamma," but the boy was called mischievous. Give your little man tools, and teach him how to use them. Let your sons have a room where they can ham- mer and saw, and paint, and whittle, and varnish to their heart's content.

They won't care to run in the streets if there is a place at home where they can be comfortable. They may make noise and dirt in this room of theirs; but when YOU want quiet le:, them cut out papers for your cake tins, showing them how to use the compasses, and if these are lacking, a pencil and string. They can cut out papers for the bird-cage, too, saving you many a precious moment when such things are wanted in a hurry. Let them cut book-markers out of old envelopes, cut- ting across the corner and slipping the cap thus made over the page. Encourage them to make scrap-books; old account books can be used for these, if you tell the boys to cut out some of the pages so that when the pieces are rasted in, the book closes properly. They will watch the newspapers and make selections of whatever pleases their fancy. History, biography, current events, natural history, inventions, electricity, anecdotes, witticisms, humorous sketches, and drawings. Surely in all these will be found plenty of material, and at least one subject to interest your boys. Give your sons a good light to read by at night, with plenty of room arNund the table. The sitting-room table can never be t,,0 large, and no member of the family should ever feel crowded out from it.
If you keep him busy and happy he will find congenial employment at home, be free from " snubs " and "don'ts," and the mother will be happy in the love and companionship of a good son.

div.head: HORSE TAMER'S RECOLLECTIONS.
div.p: A HORSE TAMER'S RECOLLECTIONS.

Captain M. Horace Hayes, well-known as a most accomplished teacher of horsecraft in all parts of the empire, has given his recollections to the public through Mr. T. Fisher Unwin, under the title of " Ameng Men and Horses." The following are some interesting excerpts from the volume:—
IRISH HOLiSE BEEPING IN THE OLD DAYS.

Captain Hayes describes "the horribly insanitary conditions " under which Irish horses were kept, even at a comparatively recent period. Horses' beds were mere dung heaps. Ventilation was carefully prevented. " Moon-blindness " was, in consequence, a common disease so were asthma, chronic bronchitis, stable fever, Sze. The worst kept stables, as far as venti- lation went, were those in which the old Irish post horses lived. I remember one four-horse coach in which there was only one eye capable of seeing with, and that belonged to the one-eyed driver. Much of the coaching was done with Bianconi's quaint-looking conveyances, which were long, large and four-wheeled outside cars. The horses of all these coaches were terrible cripples, with hardly a sound leg among twenty of them; and yet when they were warmed up with a mile or two's travel, they would face their collazs, sulde along, and stay their distance in gallant style.

IRISH JOCKEYS AND GENTLEMEN RIDERS. The Irish of Captain Hayes's boyhood regarded horses almost entirely from a jumping point of view; and horsemanship as riding. . . . They despised driv- ing, except when they were drunk and going at full gallop down a hill as steep as the side of a house. . . . . In my early days the gentleman rider was sternly repressed by the professional, who, like the Cos- sacks, Carols, Noble, and others, regarded gratuitous chase-riding as an unwarrantable attempt to take the bread, or rather the whisky, out of their mouthsr Poor Captain Bernard Shaw, who was so fond of getting a mount that he would have gone a hundred miles to ride even a loser, got killed by a couple of jockeys, who closed on him at a fence, and who had vowed that un- less he would stop riding they would "do " for him.

div.head: BILLIARD SHARPS.
div.p: BILLIARD SHARPS.

No form of sport ever came amiss to the ho rse-loving Captain Hayes. In the early part of his book he gives many reminiscences of professional and gentlemen bil- liard players. He mentions Mr. T. P. O'Connor's father as a famous player at Athlone. There was a billiard sharp, named The Dutchman, who used to pay Ireland periodical visits with much profit to himself. His game was pyramids, at which I have never seen a better player, not even Jack Roberts or Mr. Mayhew. No matter what odds he gave, our Irish players were no use with him when he had backed himself heavily. His long, and successful career with fifteen red balls and one white one, was summarily stopped one day when he was crossing a London street by a careless cabdriver who accidentally destroyed the sight of one ot his eyes by a flick of his whip. Five-and- twenty or thirty years ago there was a great deal of swindling carried on at public rooms by billiard sharps, whose occupation has now entirely departed. Few gentleman at present devote their talents to it. Taken all round, I am inclined to think that amateur play is much inferior to what it was when Roberts had rooms in Brighton, and poor Bill Cook had rooms on both sides of Regent-st. The best gentleman player I have ever seen was Mr. Myers, who used to strike terror int 9 the hearts of the Brighton pool players.
A HORSE-TAMER'S COOLNESS.

Captain Hayes entertains but a poor opinion of the common run of horse-taming professors. " Rarey, Sample, Rockwell, Hurl bert, Magner, Gdeeson, Pratt,and others were patent medicine men, who prided them- selves on the exclusive possession of some secret remedy, which, however excellent it might be in some cases, could not possibly be effective in all." The wildest horses are the easiest to break ; it is your dogged, obstinate animal, with his unsensational tricks, who needs the greatest expenditure of patience and ingenuity. Most " professors " are, in Captain Hayes's opinion, showmen. As a rule they are blessed with presence of mind. As an illustration, take the Nlowing account of an accident to Mr. Sample :—On one occasion, the great American tamer, while holding a class, got into a light trap to which a horse that ho had put through his system was harnessed. It seems that all the " stuffing" had not been taken out of the animal ; for, as it was being driven round the ring, it kicked, plunged, and finally upset the cart on top of Sample. Horror-stricken, the members of the class rushed into the ring to extricate their teacher from his perilous position. "Keep outside of the ring, gentlemen, please ! " called out Sample from under the cart, "I am just showing you how not to do it." He then hailed Joe, who pulled him out of harm's way. Sample adjusted his gear, gave the horse another dose of the "system," and drove it round in his usual fine style, to the immense delight and admiration of his audience.

div.head: THRILLING TEN SECONDS.
div.p: A THRILLING TEN SECONDS.

I remember once walking unarmed through a part of the great Nirmul jungle in India, when suddenly a tiger sprang Up almost at my feet. For probably ten seconds, which seemed as many years, he raced round me, whilst I stood still, wondering why I could not put out my hand and catch him by the tail, which was the only thought that occupied my mind during these eventful moments, until with a bound and growl the tiger dis- appeared into the thick underwood.
THE SENSATION OF BEING " CHAWED UP."

Still more marvellous were the escapes narrated in the following passage : I have known three friends who were partially de- voured by wild beasts under apparently hopeless circum- stances of escape. The first was Livingstone, the great African traveller, who was knocked on his back by a lion, which began to munch his arm. He assured me that he felt no fear or pain, and that his only feeling was one of intense curiosity as to which part of his body the lion would take next. The next was Rustem Pasha, now Turkish Ambassador in London. A bear attacked him and tore off part of his hand and part of his arm and shoulder. He also assured me that he had neither a sense of pain nor fear, but that he felt excessively anrgy because the bear grunted with so much satisfaction in munching him. The third case is that of Sir Edward Bradford, an Indian officer now occupying a high posi- tion in the Indian Office. He was seized in a solitary place by a tiger, which held him firmly behind his shoulders with one paw and then deliberately devoured the whole of his arm, beginning at the end and ending at the shoulders. He was positive that he had no sensa- tion of fear, and thinks that he felt a little pain when the fangs when through his hand, but he is certain that he felt none during the munching of his arm.

div.head: VANITY OF THE ANOLO-INDIAN AMATEUR.
div.p: THE VANITY OF THE ANOLO-INDIAN AMATEUR.
Captain Hayes has much to say about the exclusive- ness of Anglo-Indian society, and the vanity of theatrical amateurs :

As an instance of this I may mention that Mr. Rudyard Kipling told me that, wishing to make things pleasant in a report he was writing on some amateur theatricals for an Indian paper, he, trying how far he could go, said that the leadirm lady (who was really a " stick "of the most woDden sort) hv her marvellously fine acting re- minded him of Miss by Terry. On the evening of the day in which his report appeared he met the extrava- gantly praised-up one, who, instead of being annoyed with him for having chaffed her, said, " I am very cross with you, Mr. Kipling, for having compared me to Mies Ellen Terry, who is much older than I am. Don't you think that I am far more like Miss Mary Anderson ?" "I am very sorry," replied the gallant Mr. Kipling, " that I made such a stupid mistake. I ought to have said that you reminded me of Miss Mary Anderson." " Of course that was what you meant," added the lady, who graciously signified her acceptance of the journal- ist's antende. " After that," said Mr. Kipling to me, "I gave up reporting amateur theatricals."
THE " CHAMPION KNOCKER-OUT."

Like a sensible man Qaptain Hayes rejoices over the Ji:3aopearanee of the prize-ring. Many prizefighters, when they were asked to give lessons, insisted on being paid in advance for a dozen, and then gave their pupil such a" doing "in the first one, that he seldom returned for repetition of ill-treat- ment. This was a favourite trick of the once peerless Joe Nolan. And thus the goose gradually forsook its old haunts and now deposits its golden eggs for she sup- port of such admirable institutions as the German Gymnastic Club, The Orion, West London, &c. The cleverest of the clever and bravest of the brave were, as a rule,exploiteci by rascally (ironically called "sporting') publicans who used them as mere " draws" to the house, for " the good " of which they were sup- posed to take all the drinks offered or cadged for. A short course of this prostitution of manhood soon made the clear eyes blurred ; the dauntless heart " jumpy ; " and the hard athletic frame a mass of diseased fat. Even now the whisky-bottle is the champion knocker-out.

div.head: TEE TRANSPORT OF lIORSE3.
div.p: TEE TRANSPORT OF lIORSE3.

Captain Hayes strongly advises the use of coir nmttinc.r, as a protection to horses and other valuable animals being conveyed by sea. He says :—I cannot help think- ing that few, if any, of the persons wholave been in charge af rans which, like Blue Gown, Ossory, who was vvn hither to Ormonde, Prince Jo, and scores of other valuable animals, have been lost from stress ot weather whm closing the Atlantic, knew much about the virtues of thick " pily " coir matting and strait jackets for liwrses. The two great dangers to which a boxed horse is specially exposed on board ship are having the box knocked to pieces or carried away by heavy seas coming over the side ; and the horse getting tossed, dur- irg rough weather,from side to side in his box on account of his not being able to retain his foothold, and becom- ing thus more or less seriously injured. On such un- fortunate occasions, the horse w ill almost invariably become dreadfully frightened, and in his .frantic off irts to escape will dash himself about, wholly regardless of the fearful injuries which he may inflict upon himself.

HERRICK. There's no impossibility to him Who stands prepared to conquer every hazard: The fearful are the failing. MRS. HALE. On the morning subsequent to the visit of the so-called Countess of Arevalo, at an early hour, Lord Trevelyan was visited by his lawyer, with whom he was closeted for some time. The result of the interview was the production of a will, duly signed, and witnessed by the Earl of Hampton and another nobleman, both of whom opportunely called upon their old friend the marquis by invita- tion. This will as Lord Trevelyan had indicated, secured to the young girl known as Giralda Are- valo the sum of sixty-two thousand pounds, the fruits of his years of saving. When the lawyer and visitors had departed, the old lord secured the will in his bosom—the lawyer having retained a duly attested copy—drew his writing-case towards him and proceeded to write several letters, addressed to fashionable milliners at the West end. •

"Now that I have an object to spend money upon," he thought, as he had thought before, "people shall see whether lam a miser or not. I have not been able to spend my , entire income upon myself, but I have some one now to share it with me. I shall, without doubt, live many years yet, despite this attack of gout, and I intend to take comfort with this little girl who has come to me so strangely, to become the pet of my old age." _ _ _ _
-His dark eyes softened in their expression, and his countenance became singularly gentle and plea- sant.

He sealed his letters, and dispatched them to be posted by his valet, and then sank into a thought- ful mood, from which he was aroused by the open- ing of the door, and the sound of gentle footsteps within the door.

"Is it you, Giralda ?" he asked, his rugged fea- tures warmed and lighted by a rare and tender smile, such as had not been seen upon them for years. "Come and sit beside me, my child." He put out his hand and drew the young girl to a low chair beside him, and looked with a wistful tenderness into the bright, sweet face, and lovely, changeful eyes upraised to his. If the suggestion made by Lord Adlowe on the previous evening, that Giralda was the child of Geoffrey Trevelyan, had at first found a lodgment in his mind, it had now been dismissed. The dif- ficulties in the way of such a possibility had. caused him to refuse it further consideration. The reflection that the Lady Beatrice Hampton had been tenderly beloved by the supposed dead Geof- frey, and that the young couple had been betrothed, had forced itself upon him with great effect. He considered it impossible that Giralda should be the offspring of a secret union between them, and he had finally come to the decision that the maiden's singular and striking resemblance to Geoffrey Tre- velyan was merely one of those singular coinciden- ces which will arise now and then to puzzle even the wisest brains.

And yet, in the secret recesses of his soul, Gir- alda had become linked with the memory of Geof- frey, as he remembered the latter in his happy, careless, innocent boyhood. It is certain that the involuntary association of the young girl with that boyish image brought with it no aversion for the former. There was a strange tenderness and gentleness in his looks and manner now that he had not before displayed, and of which Giralda had not deemed him capable. She was learning fast, however, that under all his eccentricity, foibles, and faults, he had a heart which was slowly warming from its long frozen torpor to the noblest impulses and affections. "We shall start for home at noon," said the old nobleman, almost gayly, taking her small white hand in his. "The day is bright and we shall have a delightful journey. My foot is quite well to-day, and I shall bear the travel without pain. You look a little pale since we came to town. You need the fresh Welsh air."

"I shall be glad to go back, my lord," replied Giralda, with a low sigh for the loved ones at The Evergreens, of whom she had been thinking, and for whom at times her tender heart yearned pain- fully. • "Do not call me my lord,'" said the marquis, smiling. "You are no longer my secretary, but my adopted niece. You see I have changed the terms of our proposed relationship. I have a fancy," he added, gravely, as if speaking to him- self, to hear you call me 4 uncle. '' Giralda's cheeks flushed a little as these words, and her hand trembled in his clasp. She stole a glance up at his face, but its expression reassured her.

"I will call you uncle, if you wish it," she said, softly. "And now, uncle," she added, shyly, "if you have no especial wish for my presence, I will get ready for our journey. It lacks only an hour of the appointed time." She arose, bent over the old lord with a sudden impulse, and dropped a kiss on his forehead. The next moment she had glided from the room. The succeeding hour was a busy one. Giralda's few effects were packed, and an early dinner was eaten in the marquis's parlour, at the conclusion of which the carriage was announced, and the party took its departure for the station. The journey home was uneventful. The day was drawing near its close when the travellers alighted at the little Trevelyan station. The brightness had all faded from the sky, and the dull gray clouds had a wintry appearance. A wild March wind was blowing from the west, bringing with it the saltness and freshness of the sea. The mountains seemed outlined against the gray sky with more than usual grimness and rug- gedness, and the little village had an aspect of forlornness and death in life.

The lumbering old Trevelyatf chariot was in waiting, and the marquis, leaning on Wigby's arm, took his way towards it, groaning at every step. As Giralda followed, with her little maid, she noticed that a coachman, in faded and tarnished livery, was holding the door of the vehicle ajar. He lifted his tall, cockaded hat to her, as if he looked upon her as his mistress, and then mounted the box, while Wigby assisted his master to a comfortable position beside .the maiden. The little Welsh maid then entered the coach, Wigby climbed also to the box, and, with a grand flourish of his long whip, the old coachman started up his horses, and the old chariot rattled along the stony street.

"I have engaged several of my old servants, my dear," said the old, marquis, explainingly. "They have been living with a family near the village, but being thrown out of employment because of their employer's determination to travel on the Conti- nent, I have re-engaged them. I intend to have the Park restored to its former comfort."

As the chariot ascended the hilly street, many curious eyes looked out from the windows of the pretty villa-like cottages. Evidently the villagers were already well acquainted with his lordship's increasing liberality, and looked upon it as a piece of good fortune for themselves. The shopkeepers, especially, hurried to their doors with obsequious bows, as if soliciting the notice of the hitherto haughty and unsocial marquis. Passing rapidly through the long, single street, the coach lumbered on its way towards the Park, up hills and down valleys, leaning from side to side in a threatening manner, and occasionally brought to a stop in some deep rut, horn which extraction seemed almost impossible,

The shadows of evening -shut out .the dizzy precipices and frowning cliffs from sight long before the three miles intervening between the village and the Park were traversed, and lights, gleaming from the top of the mountain, served as a beacon to the tired travellers.

" we are almost home," said the marquis, as the coach gave a violent lurch, flinging (liralda fonvard from her seat. "Those lights proceed from the Park. Arc you very tired " Oh, no, uncle," replied the maiden, cheerfully. "It seems to me, though, that this mountain road is dangerous. A misstep, in sonic places, and we might fall a hundred feet !"

i` But we won't make the misstep These horses are bred to mountain roads, and are sure-footed beasts," said Lord Trevelyan. " I should quite enjoy the ride if it were not for the wrenchin,, my toot receives. An we are about to turn Into tne home grounds. It will be easier now." Ile leaned back with an air of relief, and the coach now bowled over the ground more rapidly, in due time the vehicle drawing up before the en- trance porch, where the travellers alighted. To Giralda's surprise, the house was lighted throughout the front, in both stories, and an air of festivity seemed to pervade the entire establish- ment. The wide, double-entrance doors were flung open, and in the wide, vaulted hall stood half-a- dozen servants, the women in snowy caps and milled alarms and the men in a faded Ereen and '

gem livery, an wearing smiles of welcome. At tne head of the servants, in a rustling black silk gown, was Plumpton, the housekeeper, fairly radiant with the change.that had been wrought in the establish- ment ; and beside her was the newly-reinstated former butler of the mansion, a pompous little man who believed devoutly in the grandeurs and glories of the Trevelyan family, and whose past year bad been spent in an unsuccessful attempt at innkeep- ing in a neighbouring village. The old hall, wainscoted with oak as black as ebony, with an oaken floor polished like glass, was festooned fancifully with holly and evergreens—the work of good Mrs. Plumpton. Giralda, astonished at the strange spectacle before her gaze, moved nearer to the marquis, who drew her arm gently within his, and leaning on his massive, gold-headed staff, conducted her into the hall.

"So you are back again Black," was the uncere- monious speech of his lordship, as he came to a halt. "I'm glad to see you. All the old servant too. Let things go on as they used to. You will always look tor orders to my niece, Miss Arevalo, who will be the mistress of my establish- ment."

Having thus made the servants of his household acquainted with their young mistress, his lordship conducted the maiden into the drawing-room, the door of which stood invitingly ajar. The apartment, of which, previous to her depar- ture for London, Giralda had had but a glimpse, was long and low, with an oaken ceiling, richly' carved and groined. Five long windows to the east opened upon a terrace, but were now closed and curtained with ample folds of amber satin, which fell in lustrous waves upon the floor. The chandeliers, with a forest of wax candles, shed a, full and glowing light. The wide polished grate held a blazing fire, the red rays of which streamed out upon the amber satin furniture, now freed from brown Holland coverings, and upon the handsome carpet and rug. An easy-chair and a sofa were drawn up to tire fire, tempting t.he returned travellers to a luxurious rest.

The contrast between the late gloom and decay was striking. Giralda felt warmed to the very depths of her lonely little heart by the change, and a bright smile chased the look of weariness from her features. Even the marquis looked cheer( d and pleased, although the change was due - only to the orders he had left with the house- keeper on the day of his departure. "This is something like it ! " he said, warming his hands over the red blaze, with an air of content- ment. "What's that rascal Wigby staring at?' he asked abruptly, catching sight of his bewildered valet in the hall. "He's surprised, eh ? all be surprised before I get through." At this moment the housekeeper entered, an- nouncing that dinner was almost ready, and that she would accompany Giralda to her room, whither the young lady's maid and luggage had preceded her. The maiden withdrew at once with the worthy dame to her own chamber, the renovatcid and brightened aspect of which pleased her. The little maid had unpacked the scanty luggage, and was now seated by the fire, awaiting her young mistress. "Let me attend upon you to-day, Miss," urged Mrs. Plumpton, eagerly. "If you would dismiss that child to the servants' ball I would dress. you." . Giralda perceived that the good woman desired private interview, and dismissed her maid at once.

"Did you ever see such a change, Miss ? " ejacu- lated the housekeeper, as soon as the door had closed behind the Welsh girl. "Six servants, be- sides the butler, the coachman and the cook ! And it's all your doings, Miss! I knew when I saw your pretty face come into this house that you would bring us good luck. The old days are coming back again, and my lord will act like & Christian instead of a wild bear I mover thought to see this day !" She looked at Giralda between smiles and tears. "My lord wrote me a letter yesterday," she con- tinued, "and told me you were no longer his secretary and companion, but his heiress to whatever he has power to leave away from his nephew. And you are his lordship's niece? That accounts for the strange likeness to the Trevelyans which puzzled me from the first. The folks at the village recognised you as a Trevelyan at church." Giralda brushed out her rings of hair in silence. The housekeeper took the brush from the young lady's hand, and gently plying it, resumed:

"I think my lord has been so miserly just to be eccentric. He hasn't seemed to have any interest in anything since poor Master Geoffrey died. But all that is changed. The plate is ordered down from the London bank, and we are to have com- pany and grand times again. But, Miss Arevalo,'' she concluded, in a lower tone, "you won't forget to speak in behalf of poor Master Geoffrey, will you?" "No, I will not forget, Mrs. Plumptcrn," was the gentle but resolute response. "I will do all I can to soften Lord Trevelyrn's heart towards his poor nephew; but I have a hard task before me,' she added, sighing. "I have left the poor lad's on your wall to remind you of your promise," said the old house- keeper. "I would die happy if I could only see that mystery of the attempted murder cleared UP, and Master Geoffrey, with a wife and chil- dren within these old walls. I can't help feeling, somehow' that he is living, and will be back some day. God help him then, unless his uncle's heart is softened before he comes." The worthy woman's tears blinded her, and she did not see the emotion her words had called to Giralda's face.

"You have more to contend with than you maY think, in speaking for Master Geoffrey, Miss Arevalo," remarked Mrs. Plumpton, after a pause. "Lord Adlowe hates his cousin. If Master Geoffrey were to come back, Lord Adlowe would never come into the Trevelyan estates, and he' thinks more of them than he does of his own soul. He's perjured himself more than once, to inY thinking, and there's worse things he would do rather than remain poor. Beware of him, Miss. He's a terribly bad man." By this time Giralda's simple toilet was com- pleted, and it was time to descend to the drawing - room. With a kind word that went to the housekeeper's heart, she withdrew from her '.:hamber.

"I am in my rightful position in the home of mY Incestors," thought the maiden, as she slowlY descended the stairs. "Lord Trevelyan little dreams of the right I have to call him uncle. 1:' will make me heiress to his savings—mistress of hi home—the entertainer of his friends. He will lover: cne and cherish me. But in the hoar he discovers... my identity—if he should ever discover it—l shall be thrust out as an unclean thing. I must noi, discovered. Discovery would bring disgrace and death," and she shuddered. "By this time paP• kno‘Ns where I am. He thinks of me in my peril', __— xis position with fear and trembling. If I sho1!1 fail! Oh, I cannot, I dare not, must not fall! Every energy must be devoted to the great end of' reconciling those two—uncle and nephew. E'rerY.', sour must see some w •u in my influence over Lord Trevelyan, whom already I love. She opened the door of the drawing-room, and- entered the old lord's presence. (To be continued).
I

To A LOVER the geography of the world resolves itself into two localities—the place where his sweet' aeart is and the place where she isn't. WHEN a stockbroker fails he " g_ocs up," wheu an oil speculator fails he "lays down," when 1k merchant fails he "busts," when a railroad fails it "gets leased," when a newspaper fails it becomes " absorbed " by some other paper, and when a plumber fails he—but then, there is no word for him. In short, in the bright lexicon of the plumber there's no such word as "fail." b "WELL, my dear, are you getting on nicely w-ts your music?" "Oh yes, mamma; last mont" when I played with my music teacher, I wa9 always a couple of bars behind. Now lam a1w334 a least three bars ahead." man had a perfect right to his own opinions. Sir Gil- bert was very approachable, nothing pleased him better than to shake hands with the poorest workman in the town. He took a lively interest in everything con- nected with religion and education, and there was not a place of worship in the town which had not at some time or other received some benefit at his hands. At one time, Sir Gilbert went through the town, and cleared off the debts on every national school in the town, going on horceback with a cheque-book hanging from his saddle. He was sure he was expressing the feelings of all when they said how sorry they were that they had lost Sir Gilbert, and they all hoped they would have in his son a brilliant successor. (Applause.) Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P., proposed a vote of condolence with Lady Greenall and family. He said by the death of Sir Gilbert, the people of the town had lost a leader and a great friend. To them, the Conservatives, it was an event of great importance because they tad lost their president. They , had lost a man who had borne high a flag, for many years, and carried it almost always to victory. It was , not necessary for any of them to use the old saying "Let there be said nothing about the dead but what is good" for of Sir Gilbert, nothing could be said but what was good. His political life began in 1847 and only closed the year before last. He began in the time of the old elections, he fought his fight well, and won, constantly sitting for this borough from 1847 to 1868. Unfortun- ately he ceased to be a member by a misfortune for a few years afterwards. He again sat for • the borough in 1874. Then came the election of 1880, when he was defeated in a tough and strong fight. They saw his dogged determinedness when he went on fighting and gained the victory again—and once again. (Applause.) He mentioned these things to them because he wanted them to think of Sir Gilbert Greena.ll as an example to themselves in the way in which they ought to fighe, and never know when they were beaten. (Applause.)—Mr. Mills seconded the pro- position.—lt was also supported by Aldermen Sutton, and Harrison, and Councillor Muir. On being put to the meeting the proposition was carried unanimously.

div.head: REFERENCE AT THE COUNTY SESSIONS.
div.p: REFERENCE AT THE COUNTY SESSIONS.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day, the Chairman on the Bench, Mr. J.J. Bleckly, said, before the commencement of the business of the court he wished • to refer briefly to the death of Sir Gilbert Greenall, and to express the sorrow with which he was sure every member of that Bench had received the news of his death. It was to them not only a public, but a personal loss. Sir Gilbert Greenall was, he believed, not only the oldest magistrate in that division, but in the whole county of Lancaster. With his death they lost one of the few remaining links which connected the past of this town and neighbourhood with the present. It was not for him (Mr. Bleckly) to speak upon that occa- sion, on Sir Gilbert's long connection with the political life of that borough nor refer to the benefits he had conferred upon it. Any movement which had for its object the moral or material improvement of the town of Warrington had been certain to receive from Sir Gilbert Greenall kindly and generous support. He left behind him very few enemies, but very many friends, among both rich and poor, and he was confident that he expressed the feelings of the magistrates connected with that division of the county, when he tendered to Lady Greenall the respectful sympathy of that court. Perhaps Mr. Buckton would convey them to Lady Greenall on their behalf.—Mr. Buckton, the clerk, said he was quite sure that the solicitors, had they been present, would have spoken in support of Mr. Bleckly'a remarks. He thought everybody in Warrington would agree with those references. Sir Gilbert Greenall and Mr. Stanton were both appointed on the County Bench on the same day, and for many years their names stood at the head of the list of magistrates. Mr. Stanton died a few years since, and Sir Gilbert Greenall had been the senior magistrate for some years. Although Mr. Greenall had not been in the habit of sitting in that court during his (Mr. Buckton's) time, he believed that he sat for a very long time previ®usly.—Mr. S. Rigby Armitage said he fully endorsed the expressions of Mr. Bleckly.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S. WALTON.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S. WALTON.

The Rev. L.J.T. Darwall, 8.D., vicar of the above church took as his text on Sunday morning the words : " He asked life of Thee and Thou gayest him a long life, even for ever and ever." Alludinc, to Sir Gilbert Greenall the rev, gentleman said that "he whose mortal part had just been followed to its last resting-place by the respectful affection of all,had indeed lived a long life in years, but not in years only. Even here below they cannot call his life ended. Ho lived on still amongst them, so long as they bad the the church he built for them the pleasant homes he had provided them, the reli- gious education he had secured to their children, and the many other benefits of his devising which the village community enjoyed. They knew him as a most liberal contributor to all deserving causes and as one who still preserved a simple mind, simple habits and tastes, even amidst all the luxuries and refinements which wealth made possible: as one who took more pleasure in home life and in the companionship of every day neighbours and humble friends than in the society of those whom the world called great. The future, surely,would prove tO be not some entirely new thing, but rather the deve- lopment of whatever was highest and truest in the pre- sent. And there they hoped and trusted that everyone who had helped and benefited others here might ever find fresh scope for unselfish service, and that everyone who had upheld law, justice, and order amongst his fellow men might enter into the divine symmetry and harmony of that better world.—At the close of the ser- vice the organist, Mr. Lane, played the Dead March in "Saul."

div.head: ST. JAMES', LATCFIFORD.
div.p: ST. JAMES', LATCFIFORD.

At the close of his sermon at this church, on Sunday evening, the vicar, (Rev. F. Slater), referring to the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, said that he could not close his ser- mon without referring to a subject which had occupied their thoughts very largely the last few days. The death of Sir Gilbert Greenall, though long expected, had deeply impressed the mind of Warrington. The death of any public man, or of one who like Sir Gilbert had occupied a prominent position for many years, must necessarily produce a considerable wave of public senti- ment ; but they would agree with him in saying that his death had done so in a very unusual manner. They all felt that they had lost, not merely a benefactor, but a friend. His kind genial manner, the ready outstretched hand, the hearty recognition of all whom he knew, how- ever humble their circumstances might be, have en- deared him to the people of Latchford and Warrington far more than his gifts, munificent though they were. God grant him His eternal rest, and give them grace that they who cherished his meinory.might like him, be ready according to their ability to help forward every good work and treat all men with gentle courtesy.— After the service the congregation stood while the Dead March in " Saul " was played on the organ. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.

The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton alluded to the late Sir Gilbert Greenall in his sermon at Holy Trinity Church on Sunday morning. He said that there had been those amongst them whose pious care it had been to love the houses of God's presence in the midst of aur people. Many also had passad away to whom in this locality this work WAS indeed a labour of love. Lord Wininarleigh, Mr. Beamont, and others who needed not now be men- tioned, exhibited a devotion in this matter that very worthily reflected the old Christian spirit. And now Sir Gilbert Greenall, like David, " full of days, riches, and honour," had gone the way of other faithful workers in the same cause. His contributions to the houses of God and to their erection in this district were too well known to require enumeration, for the renovation of that hotis of God seven or eight years ago was mainly due to his gift of £5OO. It was a similar gift of £5OO, afterwards increased, that was the means of erecting the schools in Museum-st., and it was his gift of £1.500, afterwards increased to £1,700, that made it possible to think of building the Church of St. Luke; and that was by no means all that he did in this district. What he did in Warrington was only a portion of what he did for the Church at large, for they must g 6 into neighbouring towns, and especially into the neighbouring county of Chester, if they would know the full extent of his muni- ficence. He was associated with the public life of War- rington for many years, and went in and out amongst its people in a way that gave every opportunity for the observation of his character. There are not many who have passed through the ordeal which was attached to high position in life more honourably than Sir Gilbert Greenall had done. And it might be their prayer for the young man who was now called upon to take his place, and who bore his name, that in the now sphere which was before him, with all its responsibilities, duties and trials, that he might be kept as steadfast in the path of honour, of recitude, and of religion AS thy sire who preceded him. The Dead March wits played as a mark of respect, at the evening service. sr. PAUL'S CHURCH.

At this church the Rev. H. V. Pigot alluded to the deceased baronet in the course ot his sermon on Sunday evening. He chose for his text the Words " For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers that they should make them known to their children," (['salcia lxxviii. 5). He said it would he expected that he should make some reference to the loss which they had sus- tained during the past week, hut it was not for him for several reasons to dwell at any length upon the life which had lately closed. In the first place, the fact that he was a near kinsman of Sir Gilbert Greenall made it. unfitting that he should speak in any way in praise of the work he had been permitted to do during the long span of his life ; and in the second place many membPrs of the congregation knew better than he (the preacher did) Sir Gilbert's connection with the town, and of that parish in particular.—The Dead March was played by the organist at the conclusion of the service, the con- gregation reverently standing while he did so.

div.head: IHE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 21, 1894.
div.p: IHE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 21, 1894.
ST. PETER'S CHURCH.

At St. Peter's Church, on Sunday evening, the Rev. B. Percival referring to the death cf the deceased baronet, said that the call had come to one whose name was held dear in every house in Warrington, and whose deeds of kindness and charity had extended far beyond this neighbourhood. He spoke, of course, of the late Sir Gilbert Greenall. He had not the pleasure of knowing him personally, but of that there was no need in order to know him really. They in this parish had reason to cherish his memory. Had it not been for his gener9us gift in 1887, it was more than prmbable that this hand- some church, in which they now worshipped,would not now exist. Let them pray to God on behalf of those who were bereft of so great a husband and father, and that others might be raised up to follow in his footsteps. —There was a large congregation. The Dead March was played at the close of the service.

div.head: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. ANN'S CHURCH.

The Rev. James Davies occupied the pulpit of this church on Sunday evening. Referring to the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, he said before the series of Sunday school festivities and the like had been brought to a close, over the whole neighbourhood had come a cloud of sorrow and mourning. A generous benefactor had been called to his rest. Sir Gilbert Greenall was a generous benefactor at all times, and one who realized his responsibility as the possessor of great wealth. The parish of St. Ann had much cause for remembering his kindness, for on more than one occasion he generously aided the funds of the church. Since he had been among them he contributed, together with Lady Greenall, most liberally for the cleaning of the church and school. He prayed that God might give wisdom and light and power to him who succeeded to the great and many onerous responsibilities, so that he mioht discharge his duty with favour and zeal having the fear of God before his eyes.—At the conclusion of the service Mr. Percy Randall, organist, played the Dead March from " Saul " while the whole congregation remained standing.

div.head: ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.
div.p: ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.

At the evening service of the above church, the vicar (Rev. G. AlIton) took for his text Genesis ii, 17, "Thou shalt surely die." A very familiar figure he said,had now passed from their gaze, and was interred on Friday last. They all knew to whom he referred. He was a kind friend and neighbour, helpful to all religious institutions in the town, and to that new parish from the first. Distin- guished for his generosity, kindness, and amiable tem- perament, he had gone to the grave like a shock of corn fully ripe, like flowers that shut up at the close of day— the right and joyful ending to a well spent life.—There was a good congregation, and the choir rendered the anthem " Why seek ye the living among the dead ?" Mr. W. Woodcock taking the bass solo. The singing of hymn 401, " Now the labourer's task is o'er," brought the service to a .close. Mr. E. Davies played the Dead March.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL CHURCH.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL CHURCH.
At Grappenhall a muffled peal was rung on Friday, and two full muffled peals were rung on Sunday in memory of the deceased baronet. ST. THOMAS', STOCKTON HEATH.

At both the morning and evening services on Sunday at St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath, appropriate hymns were sung, and the "Dead March" played at the close. The sermon in the morning, which was preached by the Rev. H. R. C. Vernon, was also appro- priate to the occasion of the death of Sir Gilbert Green- all. After speaking of the transitoriness of human life, he went on to refer to the loss sustained by the death of Sir Gilbert Greenall. As a public man, the preacher said, he never failed to command the greatest respect and esteem of those who had the privilege of knowing him, even of his opponents. To turn to another side of his character, a strong feature of his life was that of benevolence. Endowed with large means, he held them as a trust from God, and was ever ready and willing to help with them in whatever way he thought he could do the most good. In the building of churches for the wor- ship of God, and in the erection of schools for the educa- tion of the young, he always held out a most liberal hand. The poor also would miss a good and kind friend, for he was never slow to help all who were in need and distress, but gave them of his abundance.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, AND THE
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY, AND THE
ALLIANCE BANK LIMITED.
DIRECTORS' REPORT.

An extraordinary general meeting of the above company will be held at the Bank premises, Win- wick-street, on Thursday, the 26th July, at twelve noon, for the purpose of declaring dividends, to be payable on the Ist August and Ist November, con- firming the election of Sir Horace B. T. Farquhar. Bart., as a director, and conducting the ordinary business of the company. The following is the re- port of the directors,which will then be submitted: —The directors in submitting to the shareholders the balance-sheet of the Bank at 30th of June, 1894, certified by the auditors, have to report that the position and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £33,052 19s. 2d. brought for- ward at 31st December, 1893, the net balance of profits, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts,and rebating the current bills at five per cent., is £129,826 3s. 10d. Trom this sum the directors recommend the payment of a dividend at the rate of 19 per cent, per annum, free of income tax, for the quarter ended 30th of June, 1894, to be payable on Ist August, 1894, £47.500 ; dividend at the same rate for the quarter end- ing 30th September, 1894, to be payable on the Ist November, 1894, to the shareholders whose names shall be on the registrar on 18th October, £47,500, £95.000; leaving balance to be carried to next account 3E34,626 3s. 10d. During the past six months, the directors have acquired by purchase the important business of Sir Samuel Scott, Bart., and Co.. Cavendish-square, and also the old established business of Messrs. Shruhsole and Co., Kingston-on-Thames. Sir Horace B. T. Farquhar, Bart., a partner of Messrs. Scott and Co., has joined the Board, and the shareholders will be asked to confirm his election. Mr. E. S. Phillips, the sole surviving partner of Messrs. Shrubsole and Co., has consented to act as local director at Kingston. In order to complete in cash the payment of the purchase price of these two busi- nesses, the directors have taken £lOO,OOO from the r.serve fund, which will now stand at £900,000. The directors record, with sincere regret, the recent death of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., who had been a director of the Bank .ince its establishment as a Joint Stock Com- pany in 1865.—Alfred Turner, chairmsn. 4, Bartho- lomew-lane, London, E.C., 12th July, 1894.

div.head: FREAKS OF THE PRINTER'S "DEVIL."
div.p: FREAKS OF THE PRINTER'S "DEVIL."

Very familiar in literature is a reference to the printer's " devil "—otherwise the boy on whose shoul- ders falls a deal of the drudgery ot a printing-office waiting outside the author's study door for " copy." On him, in this particular capacity, a great deal depends,as many writers, and even some Governments, have real- ised to their sorrow. That the fate of a Cabinet has been controlled by a little printer's boy can, says "Chums," easily be proved. Some years back, when a great measure was before the House of Lords, an eminent statesman gave notice of an important amend- ment, which was committed to paper in accordance with the rules of the House, and passed through the usual channels until it reached a " devil," whose duty it was to give it to the printers. Unfortunately, however, the boy put the momentous document in his pocket,and forgot all about it. This being so, the amendment did not appear in the proper place when the time came for it to be dealt with. As soon as the omission was dis- covered, there was consternation on one side of the •House and jubilation on the other, followed 137 questions and general laughter when the truth became known. A noble lord said he thought the boy was to be commended for his intelligence. But if that amendment had been printed, and if it had been assented to by their lordships as it probably would have been—the Government would have had to resign. What the unhappy "devil"' was obliged to do is matter for conjecture Another printer's " devil" ruined, the reputation for , impromptu humour of a would-be M.P. It was the custom of the great man, when wooing a certain con- stituency, to write out his speeches, sprinkling them . liberally with " Laughter,' " Applause," " Cheers," "Prolonged cheering," etc., and invariably' using, towards the end, a sentence to this effect : " But,eent!e- men, I will not weary you (Loud cries of 'Go on ! ' Give it 'ern I' and ' Bravo--! ')." His manuscript was then put into type in the office of the local paper which supported the candidate's party, ready to be. struck off as soon as delivered, and he was supelied with proofs, from which he memorised the speech for platform use. On one occasion—it was one evening, after the editorial staff had left the office—the foreman printer gave these sheets to the "devil." with strict iejunctions to " hurry up." They were in a wrapper, and addressed to the Parliamentary candidate at an hotel about a mile away. On the was' the boy gr,e sky- larking and lost the packet, which happened to be picked up by a rabid politician "on the other side." Seeing in a moment what he had found, this man took it on the following morning to the editor of the Opposition jeur- nal, who opened it without the slightest compunction. and used the contents as the hasis of a " stin,ing " article that duly appeared in his nest issue.

div.head: ANOTHER MIRACLE AT
div.p: ANOTHER MIRACLE AT
BURNLEY.
INTERESTING TO LADY READERS.
A WARNING AGAINST FRAUD.

BURNLEY has recently furnished some astonishing instances of deliverance from suffering, and the list is continually augmented. The fame of the miracles al- ready published seems to have spread, and the accounts given by some of those who have been restored to health and enjoyment of life would appear to be incredible unless they came from the lips of the parties themselves. There is, for instance, the case of Mrs. Ann Uttley, of 54, Trafalgar-street, who was interviewed by the " Burnley Gazette."

Mrs. Uttley cheerfully dilated on the great change which had been wrought in her. "Mine's just a similar case," she said, " to that of the young lady in Hollin- greave. When I read that in the Burnley paper about her, I began to think that possibly the same means might cure me, for I had suffered just as she described it."

"Then yours was a case of indigestion also ?" "Yes, for some years. I kept having to give up eat- ing one thing and another, until I got down to almost nothing but tea and bread-and-butter. I had to drop flesh-meat, eggs, and potatoes altogether. I got so weak I could hardly walk, and I lay night after night without sleep. This went on for years, and I was beginning to feel I was done for." "And did you try nothing for it ?" "Yes, everything I could think of, but it made no difference. When I read the account of that girl's case in Hollingreave, I decided at once to get a box of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. I could see that the thing was true because I had gone through the same suffering myself. Well, I got a box of Dr. Williams' Pills straight away, and I began to feel that they were doing me good the next day. I went on steadily improving, and I've never ailed anything since. They've been a splendid thing for me." "How is your appetite now ?" "Oh, I can eat anything, and enjoy it, too, and there's no miserable feeling after as there used to be. It's a pleasure now to cook a dinner and enjoy it after. I could do this in less than a week after I begun taking the pills, and I wasn't able to do it for years before. I feel stronger altogether. Last Sunday I walked eight miles, whereas before it was as much as I could do to get to chapel and back. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills have done me a power of good and I shall never think I can say too much for them." Mr. Heaton, chemist, of St. James'-street, Burnley, was acquainted with Mrs. Uttley 's case, and her remarkable cure. The reputation of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills in the district is growing every day. They prove an effective remedy in all cases in which there is need of a blood builder and nerve restorer. They cure rheumatism, neuralgia, partial paralysis, locomotor ataxy, St. Vitus' dance, nervous headache, nervous prostration, and the tired feeling resulting therefrom ; diseases depending upon humours in the blood, such as scrofula, chronic erysipelas, etc., restore pale and sallow complexions to the glow of health, and are a specific for all the troubles peculiar to the female sex. In the case of men they effect a radical cure in all cases arising from mental worry, overwork, or excesses of whatever nature.

div.head: SHOWER OF FROGS AT THATTO
div.p: A SHOWER OF FROGS AT THATTO
HEATH..
REMARKABLE PHENOMENON.

Residents of Thatto Heath, St. Helens, were on Mon- day concerned over what was apparently a shower of frogs or toads. Shortly before one o'clock a sharp shower passed over the district and lasted several minutes. Nothing was noticed before the shower, but when it ceased, the road between Thatto Heath:Library and the reservoir was literally black with frogs. The creatures were all cf the same size, the body being half an inch long. They were alive and quickly made their way into the adjoining fields. ANOTHER SHOWER.

The greatest —excitement was manifest in Thatto Heath, St. Helens on Wednesday, there having been another shower of frogs or toads. Rain had fallen heavily in the district during the early hours of the morning, and workmen passing along the road to their work at half past five o'clock were surprised to see the toads (for such they have turned out,to be) in greater numbers even than en Monday. In fact, they could scarcely walk along without treading on the small crea- tures. They had come down with the rain there is no doubt whatever expressed. The shoals that made their appearance on Monday had practically disappeared. A correspondent on Tuesday visited and minutely in- spected the place. Very few were to be seen either on the road or in the field. This was explained by the fact that on Monday night visitors had collected the animals, and they had been taken in fifties and hundreds to St. Helens. In the crevices of the wall which surrounds the field neither tadpoles nor toads in their complete state were to be seen, and very few were noticed in the field, these having to be found by looking in the grass. On Wednesday morning, as stated, they appeared in greater numbers than ever, and the fields which are known as • the" Spout " fields, near Springfield-row, are full of the creatures. People who at first were not inclined to be- lieve the report that they had come down in the rain can now find no other supposition, and the whole of the resi- dents of Thatto Heath are discussing the phenomenon. Large numbers on Wednesday visited the place,the toads being on the road all morning. The following letter appeared in the Liverpool" Daily Post :"—Sin—ln a little work entitled 'The Rain Cloud" it is •stated that showers of fish and frogs are by no means uncommon, especially in India. Thene are also instances of showers of insects, and vegetable showers. An account is given of a shower of frogs in France (not • an inappropriate country !), near Toulouse, in August, 1804.—Yours, H. LONGUET BIGGINS.

div.head: CHARGE OF PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CHARGE OF PERMITTING DRUNKEN- NESS AT RUNCORN.
A DANGER TO LANDLORDS.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday morn- ing before Messrs. A. Thomas and T. Handley, Peter Brown, landlord of the Butters' Vaults, Brunswick- street, Runcorn, was charged with unlawfully permittinc, drunkenness on his licensed premises by serving a drunken person with a pint of beer on the Bth inst. and John Burke, Back Mersey-street, the person last referred to, was charged with being drunk in Rutters's Vaults on the date mentioned.—Both defend- ants pleaded not guilty to the charges, the landlord being represented by Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, of Warrington.

sergeant Lee stated that at about nine o'clock, on Sunday night, the Bth inst.. he was in the company of Sergeant Woolley in High-street, when he saw the defendant Burke, in a drunken condition, coming up the street. When the latter arrived at the front door of the Nelson Hotel he steadied himself against the frame-work and then fell into the bar. Almost immediately after- wards he was put out of the house and witness having advised him to go home he said he would, and went down into Church-st. and passed over to Brunswick-st., in the direction of his home. Suddenly witness lost sight of him and being convinced that he could not have reached his dwelling, he and Sergeant Woolley made a search for him. Finally they visited the Rutter's Vaults and found him leaning against the bar with a mug partly lull of beer, on the counter in front of him. Witness called the attention of the defendant Brown to the drunken state of Burke to which the landlord replied that he did not notice Burke come in, or if he had seen his condition he would not have served him with beer. The landlord then told Burke to drink up his beer and go home. The latter did so, his gait, as he went down the street, being very irregular, showing plainly that he was quite drunk. At about ten o'clock that night wit- ness saw the landlord in the street. The latter came to the police station and said to witness that when Burke entered the house he looked rather strange and he refused to serve him. The landlord added that after looking at Burke for some time,the latter asked him what the- he was looking at. Burke then told him (the landlord) that he had just got sufficierfa money for a pint of beer and promised to be quiet and go home soon if the land- lord would serve him. After this appeal Brown said he served the man with the beer.

By Superintendent Atherton: There was no difficulty whatever in perceiving that the man was drunk. By Mr. Browne : Witness did not know that after Burke had had one gill of beer it had such an effect upon him as to make him appear drunk. Neither did he know that Burke was in a chronic state of semi- drunkenness, and did not hear him express the wish to be taken to Dr. McDougall for examination. It was not witness that told Burke to drink the remainder of his beer, but the landlord. Sergeant Woolley tendered evidence of a similar nature, supplementing it by saying that Mrs. Brown,the landlord's wife, would never serve Burke either drunk or sober on account of his bad languarge. Witness had known Burke eight years. He was quite drunk on this occasion. _

P.C. Gregory testified that he saw Burke at 7.30 the same eveniog in Mersey-st. He was drunk and using disgraceful language, and witness would have reported him but when he reached the office that night he found that these proceedings were pending. Mr. Browne, in defending, said that circumstances preceding Burke's entrance into the Rutter's Vaults, as detailed by the officers, were not to be used as evidence against his client. He would not contest the veracity of those statements, but he would contend that his client did not know of Burke's condition when he entered the house, even assuming that the latter was drunk. The landlord could therefore not be convicted of permitting drunkenness if he did not know the state of the person to whom he sold the liquor. Mr. Browne, continuing, quoted the case heard last February in the Appeal Court of Somerset v. Wade which was very similar to the pres- ent one, with the exception that the person served with drink was a woman and not a man. It was here proved that the landlord did not know of the condition of the woman when he served her, and the judges upheld the decision of the lower court and dismissed the appeal. He (Mr. Browne) submitted that no evidence had been brought forward to prove that the landlord knew of the man's condition when he served him with the beer. His client was a respectable man with nothing against his character, and on his behalf he offered to pay for the summons if the police would withdraw it. Superintendent Atherton said he would leave the mat- ter in the hands of the magistrates to deal with it as they thought fit. Mr. Peter Brown, licensee of the flutter's Vaults, stated that he had kept the house more than four years and had a fourteen years' character. He upheld, in his testimony, the statement of his solicitor. The magistrates adjourned for a few minutes, and after re-entering the court the Chairman said they were satisfied that Mr. Brown, the landlord, did not know at the time he served Burke that the man was drunk. They therefore dismissed the case against him. He must, however, be very careful in future with the man. —Burke was fined ss. and costs or seven days' imprison- ment.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS CAVES IN MID-AFRICA.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS CAVES IN MID-AFRICA.

On the 10th of December, 1883, Thomson had the pleasure of drinking the waters of Lake Victoria some forty-five miles east of this outlet. But here the general good fortune of this admirable explorer deserted him. Stores began to get exhausted, and fever to fasten itself on the leader of the expedition. He therefore wisely determined, instead of going to the Nile, to turn back, through the more northern district, for the sake of visit- ing Elgon, or Ligonyi, a splendid mountain that almost reaches the snow-line. The chief features of Elgon are says Dr. Robert Brown in" The story of Africa," the vast caves that honeycomb the mountain. Numbers of them contain whole villages with their cattle. But, as the fact of their extending far into darkness shows, this could not have been their original intention. Mr. Thom- son considers that they are artifisial, and, since the material of whith those he examined consists of a very compact volcanic conglomerate, that they must have been mines at a very remote period. On this assump- tion some attractive theories have been formulated. But later investigations show that they occur in the lava as well as in the conglomerate, and are probably not artificial, but merely vast blow-holes in the mountain, which is an extinct volcano, with a crater eikht miles in diameter, and from 1,500 feet to 2,000 feet in depth. The cave dwellers inhabit the southern side of the moun tain, which is 14,000 feet high, the northern side being populated by a wretched tribe akin to the IVaelgumi, still farther north. With the exception of a few Wan- derobo, they are the only inhabitants of this mighty mountain. which, by the way, has a base 150 miles in circumference.
