div.head: SHARP BOYS AS INVENTORS.
div.p: SHARP BOYS AS INVENTORS.

If everybody had his due,the idle boy might be almost as celebrated as that well-known author, " Anon." Fcr it is at least possible that there are several more or less closed parallels to the incident of Humphrey Potter and the steam engine. Little Humphrey was an attendant on Newcomen's engine—a sort of link between the steam pump and or modern engine—and his duty was to open and close a valve. But Humphrey was an idle boy, and he saw that he could save himself the trouble of attending to his work by fixing a plug on a part of the engine that came to the proper place at the proper time by the general movements. He acordingly did so, and by his ingenuity thus made the important invention in Newcomen's engine known as the "hand-gear." Hum. phrey PottPr did nothing else that we know of; but Edison, who invented a contrivance similar in one res- pect to his,has followed up his success. When the great American inventor was a boy, he was engaged as tele- graphist at Shotford, in Canada. He was a night opera- tor. and he had to report "six "every half hour to the circuit manager. The object of this rule is obvious—it was to prevent an operator sleeping while on duty. But young Thomas rigged up a wheel with Morse characters cut in the circumference in such way that, when turned by a crank, it would write the figure six and sign his office call. As the watchman undertook to turn this wheel, the yeauthful telegraph clerk could sleep with safety when so disposed. Who can say what influence the little success of the automatic call had on Edison's future career ? A few years later, while still a boy—for he was only seventeen—the famous inventor worked at Indianonolis, where he completed his first successful telegraph instrument. It was an automatic repeater— an instrument which transferred the writing from one telegraph line into another without the medium of an operator. This was.immediately recognised as an important achievement for one so young. At this time, too, Edison was thinking about his quadruplex system—a system of telegraphy by which four distinct messages, two in each direction, may pass simultaneously over a single wire. He did not perfect it, however, until some years later. . . . Brunel, of Thames Tunnel fame, is said to have invented at the age of twelve, a nightcap-making machine, which is still used by the peasantry in that part of Normandy where he was born. It was singular that, many years afterwards, when he was about to begin the great work of his life, he made a contrivance for cutting and shuffl- ing calds without the aid of the fingers—an invention that was produced in reply to a playful request by Lady Spencer. Of living boy inventors there are doubtless many. It is well-known that working men make many time-saving applicances for which their masters get the credit ; and what is true of men is true of boys also. The writer, however, knows a young mechanic of six- teen who has already, through his father, taken out a patent for certain improvements connected with lathes. Several of the apprentices where he works are also inven- tins, but not patentees in any sense.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: DRUNKENNESS IN CHESHIRE.
A HIGH TRIBUTE TO RUNCORN.

At the quarterly meeting of the Cheshire Stand- ing Joint Committee, held on Saturday at Chester Castle, Colonel France Llayhurst presiding, the Chief Constable submitted his quarterly report. Mr. R. Bate said he noticed with pleasure in the report that Runcorn was improving with regard to drunkenness. The, number of licensed houses through- out the county was 3114 per 1,000 of tho population,and the number of persons proceeded against being at the rate of 1.28 per 1,000. In Runcorn the number of houses averaged 3.6 per 1,000, and the convictions for drunken- ness were so low as 1.06 per 1,000. Runcorn was, there- fore, almost the best, and Wirral, strange to say, almost , the worst, for there the publichouses averaged 282 per 1,000, and the convictions 1.61. Hy de was, however, I the worst with 6.50 houses and 200 convictions per 1,000 of the population. Nantwich and Crewe had a low rate —(hear, hear, from Dr. Hodgson)—this being -92 per 1,000 of the population. Why HyLie should be so bad he did not know, but he was at all events pleased to see the improvement that had taken place at Runcora. Mr. P. Speakman also expressed his gratification with the state of Runcorn in this matter. He had always maintained that Runcorn was a model little town— (laughter and hear, hear)—and it was only because of the construction of the Ship Canal and the consequent surplus population that the town's average for drunken- ness had been so high. He was sorry that Mr. Graveson was not present to receive Mr. Bates' castigatiou for the state of Wirral. (Laughter.)

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
LATCHFORD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The Sunday school anniversary services in connection with the above place of worship, were held on Sunday. There was a good congregation in the morning, Mr. J. R. Allen, of Lymm, being the preacher. In the after- noon there was a children's service, conducted by Mr. W. Brough, during which the children sang several special hymns. The Rev. J. S. Hughes was the preacher in the evening, and he delivered an excellent sermon. The chapel was crowded and the collections on behalf of the school fund realized a little over £7. SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The choir sermons in connection with the above chapel were held on Sunday, when there were -,ood attendances both morning and evening. The preacher was the Rev. J. Kirtlan, who preached two excellent discourses. In the evening the choir gave the anthem • "Be glad in the Lord," in which Miss A. Morrell took the solo portion very efficiently. In the evening service the choir further rendered the anthems "Trust in the Lord," in which Miss Morrell again took the solo portion, and "The Lord is my Shepherd," the various solo and duet parts of which being taken by Mrs. Bailey, Miss H. Brough and Mr. R. Entwistle. Collections were taken at each service in aid of the choir fund. WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

A well-attended meeting of this society was held on Sunday afternoon in Wycliffe Church. The chairman was Mr.W.Bayley. Mr.Newburr.of Manchester,delivered an address and based his remark, on the text " Wisdom is the principal thing, therefore get wisdom." The address which was an interesting and instructive one was listened to with much attenti on. The Rev. John Yonge, who has been absent for several weeks on his holidays, received a hearty reception. He thanked the members for the reception they had given him, and expressed the hope that they would keep up the good attendance. A violin solo was efficiently rendered by Mr. R. H. Pearson. 'essrs. Pendlebury and Birch also took part in the meet.nF.,..

div.head: REV. A. A. MARKHAM AND NEWSAGENTS.
div.p: REV. A. A. MARKHAM AND NEWSAGENTS.

On Sunday the pulpit at the Parish Church was occu- pied by the Rev. A. A. Markham and he chose for his text the words "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them," Matthew vii. 20. In the course of his sermon the rev, gentleman said he did not remember a single instance of a visit to the house of a parishoner when he had found a member of the household engaged in read- ing a book. People were fond now-a-days of reading a poor class of literature, althoneh for the price of a glass of beer the best novels and lives of good men were published by certain societies,notably by the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge. Certain half- penny and penny papers were devoured by readers of all ages, and as the demand so was the supply. It was to him a marvel how a newsagent with any self-respect dbuld permit the outside of his shop to be placarded by pictures so flagrantly obscene as those he had noticed during the last few weeks. It surely was a public scandal that in addition to the temptations which naturally beset 'children their minds should be poisoned and their thoughts corrupted as they walked along the streets by the sight of such openly exhibited filth. Juvenile depravity in London, they were- told, was largely to be traced to the effects of the reading of cheap and trashy literature, wtrich was so largely distributed in the streets. And they could well understand it. Last Thursday a new pile of buildines,honceforth to be known as "Fairfield Schools," was formally opened, and that morning they had been used for the first time for Sun- day school purposes. . And on the morrow they would be used as a day school. It was, perhaps, the most impor- tant event that had happened in the parish since the church was restored, and surely there was need to pray that God's blessing might rest on their work. The erection of the schools meant that they did believe in religious education.

div.p: the Gothenburg Licensing system. The meeting was called by the Duke of WESTMINSTER and amongst those present were Cardinal Vaughan, Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, and two or three bishops. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was called upon to explain the Gothenburg system apparently for the reason that he had tried some years ago to secure its adoption in this country and had failed. In the end a resolution was passed on the motion of the Bisnor of CHESTER asking the Government "to institute an inquiry as to the working of the Scandinavian system of public-house reform, and also of the canteen system in the British army, with a view to the application of similar principles in such town and country districts as may desire to adopt them." All this must be, as we have said, a source of encour- agement to the temperance reformers who have fought for their cause, in spite of obloquy and misrepresentation, for years past. But Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and those who are acting with him are going too far, in their new-born zeal, when they ask all other temperance reformers to give up their own opinions as to what reform ought to be adopted. At tho same time there is undoubtedly a great deal to be said for the Gothenburg system, and when the DUKE of WESTMINSTER and the BISHOP of CHESTER bring the political party with which they are identified to support it they may then fairly claim a very careful consideration of their plans.

LOCAL NEWS.
EXCURSION OF RUNCORNIANS TO CHESTER,

A number of workmen employed at the Sprinch Works, Runcorn, had an excursion on Saturday to Chester. Tea was partaken of at the Bull and S3irrup, and much time was spent in visiting the most interest- ing spots of the ancient city. Having satisfied their curiosity they at length returned home which was reached at about half-past ten. COLLIER'S BREAD is the best money can buy.—Ave. OUTING FROM RUNCORN TO HELSBY. •

The members of Mr. Parker's Bible Class, associated with the Camden Wesleyan School, Runcorn, on Sat- urday afternoon had a pleasant journey to Helsby in waggonettes supplied by Messrs. Booth and Sms, Run- corn. On arriving at their destination they indulged in a well-served tea and afterwards participated in various kinds of amusement and pleasure. They returned to Runcorn at about eight o'clock, all having enjoyed themselves.
COLLIER'S sell everything for the smallest possible profit.— Advt.
SUCCESSES OF WIDNES ATHLETES..

On Saturday at the Blackburn sports, St. ,Peters, Widnes, won the 440 yards race and G. Wright, Widnes, was first in the mile handicap. At Winnington, P. O'Connor, Widnes, secured second place in the halt mile handicap. At the Lancashire constabulary sports held at Old Trafford, P.C. Joseph Berry, Widnes, was third in one mile walking handicap. At Bowden, H. Barber, Widnes came in third in the half mile hurdle race and E. Gordon, Widnes, third in the halt mile handicap.
COLLIER'S BLACK BLENDED TEL. 21d.per quarter lb.—Advt. PROMOTION OF A WIDNES POST _OFFICE •CLERK..

Mr. Samuel G. Price. senior sorting clerk and tele- graphist at the Post Office at Widnes,has been appointed postmaster of Bakewell, in Derbyshire. Mr. Price hls been connected with Post Office work for twenty-four years, and has spent nineteen years in Widnes. During his stay in Widnes Mr. Price has made a host of friends who will greatly regret his departure, but pleased to see his well-merited promotion. COLLIER'S. is. BurrEn is the gem in the market.—Advt. ACCIDENT TO A Bo Y AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday afternoon whilst playing with a number of other small boys in White's field, Higher Runcorn, Charles Liudburg, aged eight years, living in Surrey- street, fell from an elevation on to some hard substance. His companions informed the boy's parents and he was removed to his home. Dr. McKenzie was summoned and upon examination said the lad was suffering from concussion of the brain. The medical gentleman bes- towed the necessary attentio'n upon the boy, and on Thursday it was reported that he was progressing favourably towards recovery. div.head: GIPSEY IN THE RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: A GIPSEY IN THE RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

On Tuesday morning before Messrs. P. Speakman C.C., and T. Handley, at the Runcorn Occasional Police Court, Benjamin Taylor, a travelling gippey, was sum- Irionc-d for being drunk in charge of a horse and cart on the 16th inst, in Moore-road.—P.C. Robinson stated that at seven o'clock in the evening of the day named he saw the defendant drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Moore-road. He was behaving in a very disorderly man- ner and making use of obscene language. The officer told the defendant to desist, but on the latter refusing to do so he took him into custody.—Fined 10s. and costs or fourteen days imprisonment.
RUNCORN CHORISTERS' VISIT TO BLACKPOOL.

On Saturday morning shortly after nine o'clock the adult members of the St. Michael's Church choir' Run- corn, started from.Runcorn Station by train for Black- pool. They were accompanied by the Rev.A. J.Jameson and Mr. Charles Pownall, conductor of the choir. At about eleven O'clock they steamed into Blackpool, and immediately after alighting from the train made tracks for the beach. Having strolled about for nearly three hours they partook of dinner at the Albion, and subse- quently indulged in diversions of many kinds. Even- tually they began their .journey home, which was com- pleted in safety. From the expressions dropped by several of the participators the outing was a decided success, and had been a source of pleasure to all of them.

div.head: IMPUDENT THEFT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: IMPUDENT THEFT AT RUNCORN.

Henry Cooke, of 40, Robert-st., was brought up on Wednesday morning at the Runcorn Police Court, befom Messrs. G. L. Davies and T. Handley, charged with stealing Mb. butter, valued 9d. the property of Martha Fryer, of Church-st.—ln her testimony the prosecutrix asserted that the prisoner ektered her shop at about five O'clock the previous afternoon and asked her for bread. She went at once into her .pantry arid returned with some food which she gave to him. He then went out and she almost immediately afterwards missed the but- ter. On discovering her loss she communicated with the police..--The prisoner was subsequently arrested and in answer to the charge told the constables that they would find the butter in his house. Ile admitted the theft. A search was made at the prisoner's dwelling and the stolen butter was found.—He admitted his guilt to the magistrates and was sentenced to gaol for seven days.
RESULTS or TME SICK NURSING EXAMINATION AT RUNCORN.

It will be remembered that the lectures at Runcorn on sick nursing some few weeks ago were followed by an examination in the Bethesda Schoolroom. The results of that examination of students have been received by Mr. Speakman, J.P., C.C., our energetic County Councillor. They show that one student has secured the highest number of marks, seven others have passed with dis- tinction, and nine are the winners of certificates. Twenty-four ladies stood for examination, seventeen of whom passed and seven failed. Those who have success- fully stood the test are :—Miss Clara Annie Littler, Mrs. Elizabeth Cooper, Mrs. James Littler, Mrs. M. A. Parkin- son, Miss Annie. Maria Mack, Mrs. Sarah Alice Davies, Miss Maude M. White, Mrs. Phillip Le Couteur, Mrs. Walter Collier, Mrs. W. Matthews, Mrs,. Esther Letitia Davies, Miss Blanch Rowland, Mrs. flarrop, Mrs. J. Scrag, Miss Mary Adelaide Smith, Miss Carrie Carter, and Mrs. J. Mort. The ladies who have passed with distinction will, in addition to the certificate, be pre- sented with a prize.

div.head: MASONIC INSTALLATION AT RUNCORN'.
div.p: MASONIC INSTALLATION AT RUNCORN'.

On Thursday evening the festival of St. John, in con- nection with the Ellesmere Lodge of .the ancient and Accepted Order of Masons, was held in the Masonic Rooms, Runcorn. After having been presented, Bro. Wm. Hankinson, senior warden, the Worshipful Master Elect, was duly installed, the ceremony being performed with efficiency by Bro. T. H. Annett and Bro. Coxhill, P.M., P.P.Gr.A., D. of C. Subsequently the newly installed W.M. invested the following brethren as his officers for the ensuing year :—T. E. Smith-Burgess, P.P.G. Steward, as ; Arthur Linaker, S.W. ; Arthur Salkeld, J.W. ; W. It. Wass, P.M.,. treasurer ;T. Annett, P.P.G. treasurer, P.M., secretary ; William Upton. S.D. ; R. R. Clarke„T.D. ; F. W. Clai ke, J.G. ; James Littler, P.M., organist ; C. W. Phillips, P.M., D. of C. : and George Hayes, t:ler. At the conclusion of this business the members die ample justice to an excel- lent supper, subsequent to which the usual loyal and masonic toasts were honoured, and various musical selections rendered. In the course of these proceedings a kandsome silver P.M.'s jewel, and a life governorship of the Cheshire Masonic Educational Institution were presented to the retiring Bro. . Smith-Burgess. The annual picnic was fixed for Thursday next, and the place selected was Llandudno. Many friends from Chester. Frodsham, Warrington and Widnes, were prcsetit at the event.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J ULY 21. 1894. A. LATE RUNCORN TRADESMAN AND lIIS DEBTS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J ULY 21. 1894. A. LATE RUNCORN TRADESMAN AND lIIS DEBTS.

DATE OF THE RUNCORN LICENSING SESSION. The magistrates, at the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, fixed August 27th as the day on which the licensing business for the division should be transacted. COLLIER'S FRESH IRISH DAIRY BUTTER, led. per lb is excellent,—Advt.

DEPARTURE OF THE REV. W. ALBERT FROM RUNCORN. It is announced that the Rev. W. Albert has vacated the pastorate of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Green- way-road, Runcorn,which he has occupied for one year, and has gone to reside at Winsford. The Rev. Thomas Braman, of Market Drayton, will succeed him and com- mence his duties on Sunday next. RUNCORN VOLUNTEER BAND.

This music-al combination, under the efficient con- ductorship of Sergeant Outhwaite, gave anoither concert in the Market-square, Runcorn, on Wednesday. A pro- gramme of choice music had been selected, and the ren- dering of the same was worthy of the highest praise. A large number of people assembled,and enjoyed the treat. HALF-YEARLY MEETING OF A RUNCORN TONTINE CLUB. The Railway Hotel Tontine Club held its halt-yearly meeting at the Hotel on Wednesday evening, when there was a good attendance of members. A substantial dinner was partaken of, previ ms to the transaction of business, prepared and served in excellent style by Mr. H. Darlington. Subsequently the business of the club was gone through and Mr. Newton, secretary, reported as to its Enancial position, the particulars of which proved of interest. A musical programme was after- wards admirably sustained by various members of the Society, Mr. Darlington presiding at the piano.
CLAIM FOR PROVISIONS SUPPLIED.

At th 3 Liverpool County Court on Tuesday,before his Honour Judge Collier, an action was brought by Messrs. Laming and Sons, provision merchants, of Liverpool, to recover the sum of £52 Bs. Bd. from Mr. C. J. Johnson, late of Church-st., Runcorn, for goods supplied. Mr. Tobin (instructed by Messrs. Mackay and Cornish) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Mr. (2. E. Nield) appeared for the defendant. The plaintiffs' case was that the goods had been ordered by the defendant for the shop in Church-st., Runcorn, conducted under the style of "M. Johnson," and that the defendant had in- timated that although the business was carried on in that name it was really his business. The defence was that the defendant was merely the agent or manager for his wife, whose business it was in reality, and it was stated that she was a minor, and having saved some money, had purchased the business, which hid formerly been that of the defendant's mother, the wife of a former Mayor of St. Helens. Mrs. Johnson, sen., had been through the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, and Mrs. Johnson, jun., had bought the business from the official receiver.—Mr. Tickle, a traveller in the employ of the plaintiffs, deposed that he only knew the defendant, Charles James Johnson, in the matter, and that he car- ried on the business in the name of "M. Johnson."—lt was suggested in cross-examination that he must have known that M. Johnson, in whose name the goods were ordered, was not C. J. Johnson, because he had been in- troduced to Mrs. May Johnson at a charity ball in St. Helens, and had placed her name on his programme for a dance. The witness admitted having written the lady's name on his programme, but stated that the dance did not come off, as she "gave him the slip." (Laughter.)—The judge ultimately found that the defendant had represented himself to be the pro- prietor of the business, and that he was liable for the amount claimed.—Judgment for the plaintiff, with costs, was entered accordingly.
INTERESTING PRESENTATION TO A WELL-KNOWN RIINCORNIAN.

On Monday afternoon the Graud Division of Cheshire, of the Order of the Sons of Temperance held their half-yearly session in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Winsford, Mr. Ed. Hughes, of Chester, presiding. There was a large assembly of representatives from the subordinate district branches of the Order, including Runcorn, Weston, Chester, Crewe, &e. F Previous to beginning the ordinary business the Chairman announced that he had a most pleasing duty I to perform on behalf of the division, and that was to recognise the long and valuable services of Mr. Thomas Cooke, the late Grand Scribe for the Runcorn branch of the Order. He was very pleased to have been selected for the honour of making the presentation, though he wished that duty had been placed in more capable hands than his own. However, he could assure Mr. Cooke that the present that was being made to him that day was not a mark of flattery, but a token of their respect and esteem. Speaking on behalf of Chester, there had been not the slightest difficulty in procuring subscriptions for the present, and he hoped that Mr. Cooke would long live to enjoy it, and that it would be handed down as an heirloom. The testimonial took the form of a handsome black marble timepiece, at the base of which was a silver plate bearing the following inscription :—" Presented to Brother Thomas Cooke, on his retirement from office in the Grand Division of Cheshire of the Order of the Sons of Temperance.—Edward Hughes, Grand Worthy Pa- triarch, and J. A. Gornall, secretary.' Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, of Runcorn, expressed the pleasure it gave him to take part in these proceedings and offer a few words in appreciation of Bro. Cooke's services. With regard to Mr. Cooke's qualifications Mr. Bisbrown had no wish to paint the lily. He had always worked for the cause of temperance generally and for the Sons of Temperance in particular. With h:m, it had not been half-hearted, hut a labour of love, and he would not now be giving up office but for the onerous duties which were devolving upon him as relieving officer for Runcorn. During the seventeen years he had held the position of grand scribe lie had displayed conspicuous ability and had thrown energy and enthusiasm into his work. Mr. Bisbrown concluded by saying that he would cherish the hope that Mr. Cooke's life would long be spared to work for the cause of temperance. Mr. Thomas Cooke, in acknowledging the gift, said he could not find words to express his true feelings. He had not worked for the cause of temperance with any other view but to make his fellow creatures physically and morally better. The knowledge that he had been of some little service was a sufficient acknowledgement for him, and he never for one moment expected to be made the recipient of such a present as that which they had that day made him. He accepted it with the greatest pleasure and lie could assure them all that he should ever look upon it as a token of their esteem and affection,and it should be handed down as a family heirloom. The work which he had done for the Crder during his seven- teen years of office had been work in which he had taken the keenest pleasure. In looking around the room in which they were assembled he missed the faces of many who were present when he was made grand scribe seven- teen years ago, and who had been of immense service and value to the order. A few of the old ones however, still remained with them and were rendering invaluable aid and counsel in working the old slop. Of these he might cite Messrs. J. Bowering, and W. Aitken (Crewe), Wedgewood (Chester), Jones, Fieesom, and Hender- son (Runcorn). In the face of so many changes, how- ever, the old craft was sailing along as steadily and as surely as of old, and every day the effects of its work- ing were being advantageously telt. Ia conclusion Mr. Cooke said that as long as his power should last he should devote as much as possible to supporting the temperance cause. He loved the Order and that love would never be extinguished, no matter what repulses they might receive. Again he wished to thank them for their kindness and consideration towards him and for the handsome testimonial.

Messrs. J. Bowering (Crewe), Wedgewood (Chester), and N. Jones (Crewe). all spoke in eulogistic terms of Mr. Cooke's services to the Order. The business of the Session was then proceeded with, and after some consideration it was decided to adopt a system for the centralization of funds. Cher matters of importance were discussed, after which a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Edward Hallsworth, of Eccles, for having attended and giving them much valuable help concerning the subject of the centralizition of funds. It was decided to hold the next Conference in January at Chester.

div.head: A. NUMBER OF PICNICS FROM RUNCORN.
div.p: A. NUMBER OF PICNICS FROM RUNCORN.

The scholars, teachers, and several friends, of the St. Luke's Congregational School accompanied by Mr. Slade superintendent ; and Mr. Cartwiglat secretary ; had an enjoyable outing on Tuesday. They left Buncorn at about .9-30 in the morning and sailed down the Bridge- water Canal to Moore. Here a field had been prepared for their use through the kindness of Mr. Roylance. Var- ious kinds of diversion were indulged in. Several prizes being offered by Mr. Joseph Speakman, senior superin- tendent. Dinner and tea were provided at the farm, and relished by all. The return journey was made in safety. —The members of the Bible class connected with the Runcorn Parish Church on Wednesday had their annual picnic, the place selected being Chester. The journey thither was made in waggonettes supplied by Mr. S. Yarwood, and a very pleasant day was spent, tea being partaken of at Mr. Norbury's, Foregate-st. During their stay in the old city many places of interest were visited and inspected with much curiosity. The party returned home shortly after nine o'clock, all having thoroughly enjoyed themselves.—The annual treat in connection with the Camden Wesleyan Schools, Run- corn, took place on Wednesday, when teachers, scholars, and friends, to the number of about 320, were conveyed by special train from Runcorn to Frodsham. Here they alighted and proceeded to Overton Hills where games of all kinds were played. Tea was partaken of at Mersey View and a pleasant afternoon spent. The homeward journey was completed in safety at about half-past eight. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON L RUNCORN CONSTABLE,

On Thursday morning at the Runcorn Police Court before Messrs. John Brundrit and A. Thomas, a seaman named Antonio Petersen, presumably of Norwegian nationality, was charged with having committed a breach of the peace by fighting in High-street,on the pre- vious day.—Superintendent Atherton explained that the prisoner was engaged on board a vessel now lying at Saltport. He had been in the company of a shipmate named William Kelly. They had quarrelled and the prisoner had been very badly knocked about, his shoulder blade having been put out, and he had other- wise sustained injuries. The Superintendent asked the magistrates to discharge the prisoner, and he wou!d then go into the charges against the other man Kelly.— The Bench expressed a desire to hear the ether case first. Consequently Kelly was put into the dock and Petersen was temporarily removed. Kelly was then charged with being drunk and disorderly in High-street on the previous afternoon and with assaulting P.C. Butler whilst the officer was performing his duty.—The con- stable named deposed to seeing the prisoners ' fighting, Kelly being very abusive to Petersen ' whilst the latter was lying on the ground. The officer caught hold of both prisoners to take them to the station when Kelly broke away saying, " I'm not gair_a t-) let you take me." Upon the constable attempting Co secure him he struck him in the face, kicked, and be- hayed in a very violent manner. They rolled over in the road together, and when the officer did eventually succeed in putting the handcuffs upon Kelly, the latter tried to break them against the wall. Not being able to do so he struck the policeman again in the face with ,the handcuffs. During the struggle Kelly tried to get a knife out of his pocket. He could not do so, however, but afterwards it fell on to the ground and was picked up by one of the bystanders. He was very drunk, but notwithstanding this fact, one private individual and five policemen were necessary to remove him to the station.—Sergeant Lee likewise gave testimony in the course of which he he said that " Kelly was more like a raging madman, and used the most disgraceful In- guage."—hinally Petersen was again brought into court and discharged. Kelly on the other hand,was fined 10. and ss. 8.1. costs on the first count and 20s. and 7s. costs on the second, or six weeks in goal with hard labour.

WATER POLO AT ST. HELENS. • Th., St. Helens water polo team, who this season had previously an unbeaten record, having won eight matches, were at St. Helens, on Tuesday night, decisively defeated by Manchester Osborne by 12 goals to 2. The winners had the upper hand throughout, scoring seven goals in the first half and five in the second half. Sharrock scored the two goals for St. Helena. The St. Helens second team beat Woolton first by 11 goals to nil.
LOCAL" GOLFERS."

On Saturday the second competition for the monthly prize took place in connection with the Lancashire Golf Club. The first sweepstake was taken by Mr. T. C. Norris with a score ot 93 less 12 —Bl. Mr. J. Fairclough scored 91 less 3-88. At the Southport Club meeting, on Saturday, the mem- bers concluded the first series of monthly c&mpeti- dons, and at the same time opened the second series. Mr. W. Pierpoint scored 115 less 25-90.

div.head: RISLEY PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.
div.p: RISLEY PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.

The Risley Primitive Methodists on Sunday held a camp meeting at Risley in connection with the congregation attending the above place of worship. There was a large gathering of local Methodists during the afternoon and evening, and. interesting addresses were delivered by Messrs. Luke Bates, Arthur Morton, William Stafford (Leigh), Roscoe (Warrington), Ezard, Joseph Taylor, and others. The choir rendered their music in a creditable manner, and the meeting was a very enjoyable one. CROQUET—GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington. Advt.

div.head: LIVERPOOL DIOCESA.N C.E.T.S.
div.p: LIVERPOOL DIOCESA.N C.E.T.S.

On Wednesday three members of the staff of the above named society visited the Wigan Agricul- ture show for the purpose of distributing temper- ance drinks suitable for the hay and harvest fields. .About 80 gallons of stokos, hopkos and cokos, were made and distributed by Messrs. Barber, Taylor and Mundin. Nearly everyone who tasted the drinks. spoke very highly of them. Three thousand re- cipes for making the drinks were also given away. In the evening a meeting was held in the Market Place, the Rev. W. E. Kingsbury presiding. Ad- dresses were given by the Missionaries which were very attentively listened to by an audience of about 400 people. SUCCESS OF A WIDNES BAND AT THE Er STEDDFOD. On Friday Gossages Soap Works' Band and the Widnes Subscription Band attended the Brass Band Contest in connection with the National Eis.teddi-od held at Carnarvon. The test piece was the selection "El Dorado" by H. _Hound. The prizes were awarded as follows Llan Festiniog (J. Gladnev) ; 2nd Natalie Vale (A. Owen) ; 3rd Widnes Subscription (A. Owen). The followine, bands were unsuccessful :—Giossages Soap Work's, Newtown, Morgan Crotntawe and Wrexham Borough. The following is a press note on the playing of the Widnes 'Subscription Band :—" The power of this band was extraordinary and the beautiful piano passages were delightful. In brilliancy of tone and promptness of attack they proved a revelation to the audience.' • "MANCHESTER GUARDIAN" PICNIC.

About 200 of the employes of the "Manchester Gnardian " printing works,lield their fourth annual picnic and sports on Saturday.. The place selected this year being Croft. The party came by train from the Central Station, Manchester, at 8.30 a.m., and arrived at Croft about 9.30. Sports were com- menced in the church fields in front of the hotel (lent by Mr. Sanicey). The programme included races, tugs of war, football and cricket matches. There was also a bowling handicap for which prizes were given. An excellent, dinner was par- taken of by the party at the hotel at one o'clock. At 2.30 the sports were resumed,and at 5.30 tea was partaken of. After tea a social evening and distri- bution of prizes took place at the hotel,when several toasts and songs were given. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. J. E. T. Allen, and the prizes were dis- tributed by• Mrs. Allen. The party returned by the 9 p.m: train from Culcheth to Manchester.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST NEW SCHOOLS,
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST NEW SCHOOLS,
WIDNES.

On Thursday afternoon the memorial stones of the Primitive Methodist New Schools,W aterloo-road Widnes, were laid by Mr. Stuart Deacon, L.L.8., Widnes ; Mr. J. Griffiths, Warrington ; Mr. J. Whit- ley, Stockton Heath ; and Mr. David Lewis, Widnes. The building of new schools has become a necessity as the Hutchinson-street Chapel friends have been placed at considerable disadvantage in carrying on their work amongst the young owing to lack of accommodation. The friends have worked very hard as during the last three years they have held three bazaars, and now as the result of their labours they behold the walls of the nes building rapidly rising. The schools are expected to cost about £1,700. Great preparations had been made for the stone laying and a spacious platform had been erected and was well filled, A procession was formed at the Hutchinson-st. Chapel, including the Sunday school scholars, and parad- ed a part of the town headed by the Mersey Mission to Seamen Drum and Fife Band. A large crcwd assembled in front of the buildidgs and amongst those present were the following : Mr. Stuart Deacon, L.L.8.9 Revs. W. J. Kirkland, W. E. Lead, B. Daine (Chorley),W. Thornley (Accrington), H. R. Didcock (Frodsham), J. W. Silcock, and Messrs. J. Griffiths (Warringtr)n`„ .1. Whitley (Stock- ton Heath), D. Lewis, A. E. Calvert, J. Miller. W. Cooper. The proceedings were °pealed by the singing of the hymn" Before Jehovah's Awful Throne," after which a portion of scripture was read by the Rev. W. Thornley, followed by prayers by the Revs. J. W. Silcock and W. J. Kirkland.

The Rev. B. Daine then gave a brief history of the Primitive Methodist Church, and dwelt on the good work they were doing. Mr. Stuart Deacon then laid the first memorial stone and declared it well and truly laid. He wished them every success in the enterprise they had taken in hand. Mr. J.Whitley,of Stockton Heath was then called upon to lay the second stone. He looked upon the event as one of the red letter days in his life and in connection with Primitive Methodism in Widnes. He thanked them for the privilege and the honour they had conferred upon him. He recollected coming to Widnes and taking part in religious services about 36 years ago in a cottage on the Marsh. He then declared the stone to be honour- ably, truly and manfully laid. Mr. J. -Griffiths of Warrington then declared the third stone well and truly laid. Mr. David Lewis in laying the fourth stone said he represented the Sunday school,the children of which had collected about £l7, making a total of about £lOO from the Sunday school alone. St,veral bags of money were then placed by children on this stone after which several bricks were laid by clhildren. _
....... The layers of the stons were each presented with a heAntifully bound , copy of the history of Primitive Methodism.
concluded the afternoon's proceedings.

_ A public tea followrd in the United Methodist Free Church schoolroom (kindly lent for tl:e occasion) to which a large number sat down to partake of the excel- lent iare provided. A public meeting was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel,Hutchinson-street,in the evening and was largely attended. Several addresses by mihistms and friends were given and action songs, Sze. were given during the evening by the Mersey Mission Band in uniform.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRA.RY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRA.RY COMMITTEE.
THE &NNUAL REPORT.

On Tuesday evening the above committee held their monthly meeting in the Town Hall, Runcorn, Mr. W. Handley, occupying the chair. There were also present Canon M. Wood, Messrs. T. Riley, S. Pope, and J. D. Jones, librarian.—The last-named gentleman submitted the monthly cash statement which showed that the receipts had been £32 16s. 81., which was inclusive of a balance on June 19th of £3l Os. 4d. The expenditure amounted to £2O lls. 10d., thus leaving a balance in hand of £l2 4s. 10d. The total number of hooks issued during the month of June, the library hav- ing been open twelve days, was 846, which was made up as follows :—Reference department, 14; lending : theology, 10; philosophy, 3; science, 32; history, &.,, 39; poetry, 2; fiction, 662; miscellaneous, 84. These figures show a decrease in the lending department on the corresponding period of last year ot 116; and of 9 in the reference department. The Secretary also reported having received the following gifts during the month :—By Mrs. Redgrave, "Life of Rickard Redgrave C.8.R.A." By Messrs. Mevin Bros., publishers, "The proceedings of the International Maritime Csngross, London, 1893." By the Isle-of-Man Steam Packet Co., Hall Caine's " Little Man Island." By the Working- men's Lord's Day Rest Association, " The Sunday Problem," paper presented at the International Congress on Sunday Rest, Chicago, 1893. By the Trustees of the British Museum : Catalogu. of Bird's, volumes 22 and 23; catalogue of Mesozoic Plants in the department of Geology—" The WeAlden Flora," part 1: monograph of Lichins found in Britain, being a descriptive catalogue of the species in the Herbarium of the British Moseura, part 1. LIBRARIAN'S REPORT.

, Mr. Jones submitted the twelfth annual report from which it appeared that 716 borrswers' tickets had been issued during the year, being an increase.over the previ- ous year of 12. The library had been open for the issue of books 242 days, and 21,214 works had been taken out which was 435 below the number issued last year. The average daily issue was 90 volumes. It was neteworthy that the decrease was almost entirely confined to fiction. 'The classes showing a decrease were : Fiction, 745 ; theology, 15 ; philosophy, 7 ; poetry, 2 ; whilst the following showed an increase: Miscellaneous literature, 176; science and art, 136 ; history, biography, and travel, 32. There had been added to the library during the year, 325 volumes, 294 of which had been purchased •1 and 31 presented. The total number of books in the 1 library now was 7,313. The reading rooms were daily frequented by large numbers of readers, and often more than could be comfortably accommodated. A larger room would soon become a necessity. An attempt had been made during the year to secure as many works of local interest as possible ; and in addition to the purchase of Ormerod's " Cheshire," Mr. John Simpson had presented several books and pamphlets bearing On the history of the district. It was hoped that other people would be induced to co-operate in securing for the library any literature of a local character, whether of the present ot• former generations. In conclusion, the committee ex- pressed their thanks to the various donors for their valu- able gifts of money, books, periodicals, and newspapers. From a tabulated statement appended to the report it appeared that there were 846 velumes in the reference department and 6,467 in the lending department. The last number was classified thus : Theology, 492; philo- sophy and political economy, 177; science and art, 725 ; history, hiographs and travel, 1,834 ; poetry and the drama, 148; prose fiction, 2,300 ; miscellaneous Were- ture,736,French literature. 55.—The report was adopted, and it was resolved that 100 copies be printed. The advisability of more perfectly ventilating the reading-room was mentioned and aftir some discus- sion it was decided to test a couple of iifferent burners which, it was calculated would not only throw out less heat but produce a brighter light. In the course of this discussion Canon I'Vood asked the Chairman if it would not b 4 possible to engage a suite of rooms at the Tech- nical Institute when it was completed. The Chairman replied that he did not know that they would, but he thought the matter was being considered.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA PRIZE CHOIR IN LONDON.
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA PRIZE CHOIR IN LONDON.
WINNERS OF TUE SECOND PRIZE AT THE CRYSTAL PALACE.

The members of this choir, accompanied by Mr. John ilolford, their conductor,journeyed from Run- corn Station on Friday evening to London for the purpose of taking part in the Tonic Sol-Fa Festival, held on Saturday at the Crystal Palace. A number of other Runcornians bore them company to the Metro- polis, and on arriving there wished them every success in their competition at the Place. The choristers, after making the necessary preliminary arrangements, and having refreshed themselves turned in the direction of Sydenham, where the Palace is situated. It was noticed, on entering this vast pile, that the event which was ' about to take place was evidently one of the most im- portant of the year. The attendance was very large and at the conclusion of the proceedings no question could be raised of the artistic result heir'," superior to that of last year. The programme commenced with a glee- party competition, at which Mr. J. A. Birch was the adjudicator. There were five entries, and each choir had to sing " The Shepherd's Lament " (H. Smart) and a piece of its own selection. The cotripetitors,with their respective conductors, performed in the following order :—" Excelsior," Glee Union, Mr. G. Day Winter ; " Troubadour " Glee Union, Mr. G. Day Winter ; Abertawe glee party, Mr. Evan Sims ; Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa glee party, Mr. J. Holford ; Mr. Mellis's Sol-fa glee party, Mr. J. B. Melds. There were two prizes, viz., let prize: £lO (given by the President) ; 2nd prize, £5 (given by Sir Godfrey I:ush- ington, K.C.8.). The piece selected by Runcorn was Dr. Hile's " Hushed in Death." The first prize of £lO was awarded to Mr. J. B. Mellis's (London) Sol-fa glee party, the second of £5 going to the Runcorn glee party' conducted by Mr. John Holford. The concerr by 5,000 ! certificated juvenile singers took place at one o'clock. This army consisted of contingents drawn from sixty- five school and evening-class choirs, and a combined attendance having been impossible until Saturday, the attention and precision given to the entry of parts and the general attack by the powerful singers showed that considerable pains had been taken at the numerous dis- trict rehearsals. The entertainment, ably conducted by Mr. George Merritt, Mr. J. F. Proudtnan bring the organist, went without a hitch, and the thirteen items were all sung in an admirable manner. Three, indeed, were so loudly applauded that they were repeated. just before four o'clock was held the concert by the 3.000 adult singers, some of whom came from Runcorn, Leeds, Sheffield, Halifax, Manchester, Hull, Grirnshy, Nottingham, Reading, Kidderminster, Birmingham. Swansea, Bournemouth, and other principal towns. The first part was devoted to a new sacred cantata, by Mr. Coward, entitled Time King's Error." The next nest piece, also encored, was Madame Clara Samuell's solo, " Let him that taketh the field.' The soloists, three of whom are well known in London, Madame Clara Samuell, Mr. J. Gawthrop, and Mr. Rob- ' Grice, may be complimented upon their tasks, whilst . the bass, Mr. Charles Siebert, did excellent service. The Crystal Pakce orchestra was augmented for the occa- sion, and the instrumentalists played steadily. At the close Mr. Coward was the recipient of an ovationon the personal introduction to the metropolis of a work of which he may be proud. After the day's exertions the Runcorn party pro- ceeded to their variems apartments to rest. A large portion of the next day was spent in visiting several well-known places of worship, St. Paul's Cathedral and Westminster Abbey being foremost among the number. On Monday many other parts cf the great city were visited, including the Tower. Monument, Tower Bridge, Mint, &c. They were also shown through the House of Commons by Mr. J. T. Brunner, the popular M.P. for the division, who had heard of their success at the Crystal Palace. He warmly congratulated them noon their fine performance at the festival, and expressed an earnest wish that they world attain to a still higher position in the musical world in the near future. The return journey commenced in the small hours of Tuesday morning, and was completed shortly after seven o'clock, everyone arriving home in perfect safety.
A RUNCORN DOCIOR NARROWLY ESCAPE. BEING SHOT.

A providential escape from what might have proved very serious injury was experienced by Dr. MacLennan, of Runcorn, on Friday morning of last week, and the circumstances ought certainly to act as a warning against careless possessors of firearms. At abou t eleven o'clock in the morning the doctor was driving in his trap to Weston there to attend a patient. who required his urgent attention. On reaching the Slide, Higher Run- corn, he heard the rep,:at of a gun, and almost at. the. same time his right hand was struck by several small pellets. The glove on his right hand was slightly cut by the pellets, and both he and his groom were somewhat alarm-d. The pony also shavd their feelings, and needed all the &kill Dr. MacLennan to control the animal. However, as the case which the doctor was going to was of a pressing nature he had no time to spend in making inquiries. The direction from Wilf!lle3 the shots came was the field or garden between Crofton Lodge, and the road leading to Weston. It is to be hoped that those Persons p,s..:essing shooting- privileges in this or any other locality, will exercise the utmost care when using such dangerous weapons, and that this will more especially to the case when they are near any public 1.17 g

div.head: COUNTY COURT ACTION BY A RUNCORN
div.p: COUNTY COURT ACTION BY A RUNCORN
FLAT-OWNER.
SUCCESSFUL CLAIM.

At the Liverpool County Court on Monday, before His Honour Judge Shand, Messrs. W. Bate and Co., flat-owners, carrying on business at Runcorn and Bootle, sued J. Gordon, general dealer, of Chapel- works, Liverpool, f3r £ll 103. 6d. for hire of a Hat arid damages for detention of the same. Mr. Mulhol- land, instructed by Mr. C. E. Nield, appeared for the plaintiffs, and the defendant conducted his case in perso. The plaintiff claimed the sum of £4 45., less 13s. 6t advanced to the captain of the flat, for hiring, and _-‘2B damages for the detention of the same from the 19th to the 30th May last. The defendant, it appeared, had been for some time in the habit of hiring the plain- tiff's flat Stanley at the rate of £3 10s. a week, but owing to some difference which arose as to the way defendant dealt with the flat the plaintiffs told him verbally that if at any future time he required the flat he would have to pay him £1 is. per day. On the 12th May defendant hired the flat, and on the 16th he again hired it, and on both these days the plaintiff had charged hirn at the rate of £1 is. per day. Defendant, however, contended that the flat was hired on the usual terms, vii., at the rate of £3 103. per week, and that he was entitled to the use of the flat until the 19th of May. On the 19th May, the plaintiff having previously removed the flat from the Alexandra Dock to his own place at the Carriers' Dock, the defendant moved it back, and did not return it until the 30th May, having thereby detained it for eleven days. Defendant had paid into court £4 103. 6d., being £3 103. for the alleged week's hire, 103. 6d. for detention. and 10i. for costs. The defendant's defence was that he hired the flat on the usual terms of £3 103. per week. The judge held, how- ever, that the defendant was not justified in removing the flat, and gave judgment for the plaintiff for £4 4s. beyond the amount paid into court.

div.head: OLD-AGE PENSIONS AND THE LIQUOR
div.p: OLD-AGE PENSIONS AND THE LIQUOR
TRADE. A REFORM IN THE GOTHENBURG SYSTEM.

On the same day that Mr. Chamberlain was advocat- ing in London the cause of moderate reform on the lines of the Scandinavian system, the Norwegian Legislature adopted a law introducing some important alterations. The principle of entrusting the liquor trade of each dis- trict to a public company, in whom the licensing author- ity is exclusively vested, is confirmed and extended,but material changes are made in the distribution of profits. It is one of the favourite arguments of the opponents of the Scandinavian system that, inasmuch as the profits have been hitherto largely applied to purposes which would otherwise be defrayed out of rates, there must be and often has been, a tendency, on the part of the rate- payers, through their representative bodies,to encourage the sale of drink, and generally to increase the profits of the trade by methods clearly incompatible with the pro- fessed objects of the • system. In future only 15 per cent, of the profits will go to the Communal Treasury, 20 per cent. to the company for distribution amongst temperance and other charitable institutions, after pro- viding the legal rate of interest on capital, and the balance—namely, 65 per cent.—will be paid over to the State for the formation of a special fund, of which the application is to be specified at a later date. It is gen- erally understand that this fund will ultimately be devot- ed to the creation of old-age pensions.

div.head: SALE OF WORK AT WARRINGTON RECTORY.
div.p: SALE OF WORK AT WARRINGTON RECTORY.

On Thursday afternoon, a sale of work to secure a portion of the debt remaining on the St. George's Mission, Warrington, was opened in the Rectory garden, by Mrs. Stanton, of Thel wall. The articles for sale were in two large tents, in addition to a small one which contained the 11,,wer stall. The following were the stallholders :—General stall, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. W. Woods (Fennel-street), Miss. Gray, Mrs. R. T. Fairclough, Mrs. John Walton, Mrs. Fairclough, Mrs. Wilcocks, Misses Percival, Miss Nannie Fairclough, Miss Walton, Miss Jackson. and Miss Wilcocks ; flower stall, Mrs. White and Miss Cash ; refreshment stall, Mrs. Wm. Gill, Mrs. A. Woods, Mrs. A. Browne, Misses Gill, and Miss Mainwaring. There was a good number present at the opening, ceremony. In addition to Mrs. Stanton there were pre- sent the Rector and Mrs. Willis, Rev. H. V. and Mrs. Pigot, Rev. B. Percival, Rev. A. A. Markham, flev.G.B. Thurston, Captain Buckton, Dr. White, Coumcillor A. Woods, Mr. J. Walton, Mrs. Darwall, Mr. W. Gill, Mrs. Sharpe, Mrs. Beaman, and Mr. J. Banner. The Rector in introducing Mrs. Stanton. said that he was sure that those present would be interested in knowing something about St. George's Mission. Three years ago the foundation stone was laid by Lady Walker, and the building was 'opened six months afterwards by Bishop Royston. The building had some excellent rooms' and the work had been chiefly in connection with the Sunday school. There were also Sunday evening services, a men's club and other institutions in connection with the place. It was through the zeal and energy of Mr. Jack- son to a great extent that those beautiful buildings had been erected and the work carried out, and they were greatly indebted to him. The work was now in charge of the Rev.G. B.Thurston who seemed quite equal to the task. The cost of the buildings was £1,910 composed of £1,400 for the - building and £5lO for furnishing, &c. The receipts up to the present had been £1,760, £1,260 of which had been subscribed and collected,and £5OO had been received in the form of a loan from Mr. Wm. Gill. They therefore required £175 that day to wipe out the debt and pay the expenses of the sale of work. He hoped that they would be able to realize that sum. He would like to read out some of the subscriptions which had been received. The patron of the parish had given £5O, the late Lord Winmarleigh, £4O ; Sir Andrew and Lady Walker, £5O ; the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, £220 ; Mr. Mortimer, £l5O ; and Mrs. Beaman, £l5O. They were greatly indebted to Mrs. Stanton for the many kind- nesses they had received from her, and he had great pleasure in asking her to declare the sale open. Mrs. Stanton said that she knew that very good work had been done at the mission, and she hoped it would be very successful. She now declared the sale of work open. A vote of thanks was passed to Mrs. Stanton on the motion of Councillor A. Woods, after which the business of the sale began. During the afternoon, the Blue Coat School band played selections of music on the lawn. A tennis tournament was held at which there were 60 entries. The arrangements were in the hands of Messrs. Stanley Wright, F. Taylor, A. Browne, A. Wcads and is. Fairclough (secretary). The decorations were in the hands of Mr. H. Hayes. Just before dusk, a fire balloon was sent up from the grounds. The sale will be con- tinued to-day, when the final of the tennis tournament will be played.

div.head: SID DROWNING CASE NEAR ST. HELENS,
div.p: THE SID DROWNING CASE NEAR ST. HELENS,
NO LEGAL LIXBILI eY—AS USUAL.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on Thursday morning at the Owl's Nest, Black- brook, on the bodies of the two children, George William Armstrong,aged four,son of William Armstrong, collier, Carmill-lane, and Edwin Austin, aged six, so' of Thomas Austin, collier, 16, Copperhouse-row, near Haydock, who were found drowned in the Sankey Brook Canal, Parr, on Monday evening. Mr. Bland, of the solicitors' department, Lime-street, represented the London and North-Western Railway Company, the owners of the canal. Evidence of identifica- tion was given by Elizabeth Armstrong and Emma • Austin, the mothers of the deceased children. The former stated that there was sonic waste land between their house and the canal, and there was no fence between the road and the waste land, nor betwoen the waste land and the canal. She was always afraid of the children getting into the water.—Mrs. Austin said she had never seen her son near the canal before. On the Friday she had beaten him for bashing in an adjacent dam, and he had promised not to go near the water again.—John Lievesley, of Blackbrook, deposed to seeing the bodies got out of the water. The body of Austin was recovered by himself between five and six o'clock ou the Monday afternoon after dragging operations. The other body was found an hour after about two yards from the first. The canal and the waste land being unfenced made the place danger- ous for c‘Aildren, but people were not supposed to go there.—The Coroner asked who the land belonged to.—The Foreman (Mr. P. Ball, of Ashton) said he was the tenant of the land, but it was the property of Lord Gerard. The land was in Parr. 'The Coroner: Then these bodies were found in Parr, they lived in Ashton- ! in-Makerfield. and were holding the inquest in Baydock. (Laughter.)—Sergeant Be said the spot was at the corner or the three townships. He had failed to find an' witness who saw the children mar the canal side. 'The children were in the habit n 1 going to the place to catch jacksharps.—The CorOner said he did not see from the legal standpoint how anyone could be called upon to do anything because any person leaving the highroad became a trespas3er.—The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." adding that there was no evi4ence to show how the children got into the water. They did not suggest anything, but the foreman had promised to see Lord Gerard's agent and try to get a fence put no at the roadside.—The Coroner : That is a sensible ti;ing to do.

div.p: THE COLLIERY DISPUTE AT ST. HELENS. THE NO UCES ADJOURNED.

On Monday afternoon, at Wigan, representatives of the Masters' Defence Assiociation, with Mr. T. R. Ellis as secretary, met a deputation of workmen from Ash ton's Green Colliery, St. Helens. where notices terminat.ug conttacts that day .had been served on the masters. The men were accompanied oy Mr. T. Glover, M.P., miners' agent, St. Helens, and Mr. T. Aspinwall, Wigan, representing the Miners' Federa- tion. The disputa was with regard to the consolidation of field prices, an agitation having been commenced about nine months ago. At the meeting on Monday no Settlement was arrived at, but it was decided to adjourn the notices for a fortnight. In the meantim?,, the mas- ters' representatives will recommend the directors to consolidate the present field prices and " extras " paid since 1891 into one field price, practically what the men demand, and what they would be prepared to accept. should the directors refuse to agree to the recotnmenda- tion it is almost inevitable that a strike will take place, and 500 men be thrown idle. Toe result of the represen- tative meeting was on Monday night conveyed to a full' meeting of the men employed at the colliery, and they agreed to work on for a fortnight.

div.head: ALLEGED GAMING IN A WARRINGTON PUBLIC-HOUSE.
div.p: ALLEGED GAMING IN A WARRINGTON PUBLIC-HOUSE.
RESULT OF THE APPEAL.

At the County Sessions House, Islington, Liver- pool, on Wednesday, before Sir W. B. Forwood and nine other county magistrates, the appeal of Thos. Burke, landlord of the Bird-in-Hand beerhouse, Warrington, against the conviction by the Warrington magistrates and also having his license endorsed, for having permitted gaming to take place at his house on May sth,was heard. Mr.Collingwood Hope,instructed by Messrs. H. B. White and Sons, appeared for the jus- tices, and Mr. Mulholland, instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne, appeared_ for the appellant.

Mr. Colfingwood Hope, in Opening the case, stated that the appellant's house was visited by Inspector Spinks, Sergeant Taylor, and Constable Delahay, on Saturday night, May 5, at nine o'clock. The officers went to inquire into the cause of an accident to a man. named Cunningham, who had had his leg broken, and had been taken to the Infirmary. Inspector Spinks asked the landlord about it, and the landlord told him that Cunningham was playing dominoes for beer, and that he had had a dispute over one of the games. A row arose in the house, and Cunningham had had to be put out of the house into the street,where his leg was broken. Inspector Spinks asked the landlord if he knew that he was acting illegally by permitting gaming to take place for money or for money's worth, and he replied that he did not know that he had been doing wrong. He would however, undertake that it should not occur again. Counsel proposed to call the men who were playing dominoes,and it would then be for the justices to decide whether the conviction was right, and if right to dis- miss the appeal. Inspector Spinks was then called and bore out his counsel's statement, with the addition that he also told Burke that he would be liable to a penalty of £lO for the first offence. and £2O for the second. On being cross-examined by Mr. Mulholland, _lnspector Spinks
. _ . . _ admitted that dominoes were played in almost every public house in Warrington,and that of course,the game itself was lawful. He also gave the appellant a good. character.
Sergeant Taylor and Constable Delahay also gave cor- roborative evidence.

William Cunningham stated that he was in the house on the night in questien and had one glass of beer served . him by the landlord in the kitchen. He afterwards went into the front room and being joined by three others, they agreed to have a game of dominoes for a gill of beer to be paid for by the" last man in for the first man out." They played two games and witness lost one. He ordered the beer from the appellant's daughter and she served him and he paid her 3d. He was quite positive that neither the landlord nor his daughter, nor anyone in his employ had any knowledge whatever that they . were playing for beer. He Rever saw the landlord in the room at all while they were playing. Mr. Hope was proceeding to question this • witness, when objection was taken hy Mr. Mulholland Who cone." tended that counsel could not cross-examine .Ns own. , witness, but must be bound by his evidence._ This c0n..., tention was upheld by the bench. Thomas Kelly was then called by Mr. Hopei and that he was in the house on the night of the allege/ -45' offence, and had been there about an heur. He was of those who were playing for the gill of beer. Heswore• that no one heard them make it up to play for thedieer, and further swore that neither the landlord nor his daughter knew that they were playing for beer; also that the landlord was never in the room during the time that they were plain g dominoes. • Mr. Mulholland for the appellant said that this Was ' one of the most paltry cases for any bench of magis- trates to even convict upon, let alone to endorse the. license for the first offence. He contended that his learned friend had confuted his own case by the last two witnesses called, and was evidently afraid to call the other two who were in the house, both of whom had been subpcenaed by him. He did not dispute the facts as proved by the two witnesses, as it was exactly his case. The landlord was never in the room while the game of dominoes was being played, and it was well- known that dominoes were played in public-houses, and were not in themselves proof that gaming was taking place In this case, there was no outward sign of any betting taking place, and as had been proved by the witnesses themselves, the beer was simply ordered "Two glasses . of beer, please." He contended that the appellant was not liable for/permitting gaming unless he had actual knowledge that it was going on. He quoted the case of "Somerset v. Wade," decided this year at the Queen's Bench Division, that under the section of the Licensing Act, a publican was not liable for permitting drunken- ness when he had no opportunity of seeing that the man . was drunk. That case was on all fours with the present case, in the section under which the conviction had taken place. The word " permitting" of course implied i knowledge, otherwise it could have no meaning. He contended that if the landlord did not know that gam- ing was taking place, he could not now be convicted, ar'...le would prove that neitner the landlord nor his daughter knew that the beer was being played for. With regard to the conversation between Inspector Spinks and the appellant, the appellant said that he , only knew of the quarrel about playing dominoes for beer, after the ejection of Cunningham from the house. Counsel contended that not only the endorsement of the license should be removed, but also that the conviction should be quashed. Thomas Burke, the landlord, was then called and bore out Mr. Mulholland's statement. In cross-examination. he admitted that until the night of the disturbance, he did not know that dominoes were not allowed to be played for beer. He had since removed the dominoes altogether. Mary Ann Burke, the daughter, stated that she served the customers on the night in question,and noticed them playing dominoes as they often did, but she never heard any bet made nor did she know they were playing for beer. If she had known ,she would have told her father, who was in the cellar, as she had been nine months previously at another public house, and there learned it was wrong. John Carr, bricksetters' labourer, said that he had been sobpcenaed by the respondent. ' He was playing dominoes with the two witnessed called by the respond- ents, on the night in qaestion,and lie corroborated them to the effect that the landlord was never in the room while the dominoes were played,and also that they made it up in private to play for the glass of beer. Witness lost the last game,and went out into the yard with Cun- ningham, where they commenced quarrelling about paying for the beer. The landlord then came and ordered them out, and on getting on to ) the footpath, Cunningham slipped and broke his leg.—Cross-examined: He admitted that he had been fined on Monday last ss. for playing cards, and that such fine had bean advanced by Mr. Browne. Mr. Mulholland asked if Mr. Hope was going to con- tend that there had been subornation of perjury, as the matter was simply that Carr was an important witness and to save hum from going to gaol in failing to pay the fine, was advanced out of money to be paid him for attendance at the Quarter Sessions. Mr. Hope said that he had not the slightest imputation to make, and witness thereupon left the box. ' The magistrates retired and in a few minutes returned ' and the chairman announced that the conviction had- I been quashed, and ordered the justicee' costs to be paid 1 out of the county fund.

div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Wright (chairman) Messrs. J. H. Fleming, and S. Wright. SLEEPERS ()RT.—Three strangers in the town named William Thompson, John Hunt, and Thomas Clarke were charged with being found sleeping on a haystack belonging to John Wainwright. P.C. Loxham, who prayed the case, stated that in company with P.C. Leonard from complaints received they went to Mr. Wainwright's haystack at Arpley and there found the prisoners sleeping. The hay was scattered about in all directions. The men were brought to the Police Station Mr. Wainwright said the damage done by the prisoners would be s bout 53. The magistrates imposed a fine of 53. including costs or seven days imprisonment. UNFRIENDLY NEIGHROURS.—EIIen W hite, Gilbert-st., was summoned by Alice Charnley, Howley-lane, for using threats to her on the 6th inst., and a cross- summons was issued by Mrs. White charging Mrs. Charnley with assault on the same date. Mr. Browne, solicitor, appeared for Charnley, and Mr. P. Davies represented White. The magistrates after hearing several witnesses on both sides, dismissed the cases, each party to pay their own costs. MAINTENANCE ORDElL—Nicliolas Flannery, dagger, Colne, was summoned at the instance of Mr. Shearer, on behalf of the Warrington Guardians, to show cause why he should not contribute towards the maintenance of his mother, who is at present an inmate of the Warrington Workhouse. Mr. Shearer applied for an order for is. 6s" , per week. The defendant stated that his wages were only Li per week, and he was a married man. The magistrates ordered him to contribute is. per week. CHARGE OF USING THREATS.—Jos. Brookes, 2 Gandy's- yard, was summoned by Jane Ackers, 1 Gandy's Walk, for using threats towards her on the 9th inst. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, appeared on behalf of the complain- ant. He seated that on the date named, the complain- ant had given certain information to Inspector Norman and Inspector Church, in consequence of which, the latter inspector went to the defendant's house. After his departure the defendant came to the complainant and , threatened her. Evidence in corroboration of Mr. Browne's statement was given by the complainant and her husband, and another witness. The defendant denied using threats, and also repudiated the act alleged. Two witnesses deposed that no threats were used. The magistrates dismissed the case. Asssur.T.—Thomas Davey, Albert-st., was fined ss. and costs for assaulting Dagnall, Oliver-st., on the Bth July. Ths complainant stated that on the date named he was struck in the mouth by the defendant when he went to ask him about some imputations he had made about witness's wife.—Robert Hankinson gave corroborative evidence.—The defendant denied striking the man, but the witness he called for the defence ad- mitted that the defendant did strike the complainant. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. John Burgess (chairman) and Mr. S. Chandley. A DISORERLY PAI7PER.—A young woman named Mary Jane Conway. an inmate of the Workhouse, was charged with wilfully breaking two panes of glass at the Workhouse, doing damage to the extent of is. 4d., and .was also charged with assaulting George Dobson, clerk at the Union, at 6.20 the previous morning. Mr. Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians, and stated that the prisoner was almost an habitual inmate of the Workhouse, having been there 26 weeks during the past nine months. Whilst in the house she had been very troutlesome. The previous morning she refused to do any work, and an officer was told to put her into a place of confinement. The prisoner then got a bucket of water and threw it on the officer. She also broke two panes of glass, and was an example of everything that was bad to the other inmates. The matter was re- ported to the House Committee, and they were unani- mous that the case should come before the magistrates. She was committed to gaol for one month with hard labour.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Annie Ryan made her 15th appearance before the magistrates, charged With being drunk and disorderly in Blittermarket-st. the previous night. The magistrates sent her to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.
MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Mr. J.W. Hayward, and Mr. S. Wright.

CRIIKLTY TO A rloßsE.—Edward P.urke, 5, Turner-st., was fined 10s. and costs, for working his horse while in an unfit state on June 19.—P.S. Cheney stated that the • prisoner was driving the horse along florsemarket-st. agd Bewsey-street, and as it appeared to be un- easy, witne,ss examined it. He found a sore on the back of the horse, and also on the near side. Witness ordered him to take it home, which he did. He was summoned to appear at the court, but failed to appear, and a warrant was iFrued for his apprehenson. DRUNKENNESS.-14'or this offence, Lawrence Mannion, 21, Lawrence-st. was fined 55.; Charles Jones and Mary A. Jones, 21, Albert-terrace, Howley, 2s. 61. each. CARD GAMBLING.—Four young men named John Carr, 12, Percivars-fold,Bernard McNamee, 31, Dolman'A-lane, Thorriaa 11:•rkin, 12, Percivaltolcl, and Bernard Roarke, 17, Dolman's-lane, were all charged with gambling by playing with cards in Cloth Hall-yard on the 11th inst. P.C. Bell who proved the case deposed that from in- formation given him he proceeded to an entry leading out of Thitter:narket-street and Cloth Hall-yard. He watched the four defendants for some time, and saw ! the defendant Carr win two games at cards, and to talv) money from the other defendants. The magistrates fined oath defendant ss.

He also saw the windows she had broken, and brought her t., the police station and locked her tip.—Mary Curry, wife of the complainant, said that the prisoner came to her house in Hopwood-,4*.. and omn.. menced calling her nams and threltening that she would "do three mouths" tor her. On Monday she left the Workhouso. got drunk and committed the offenc.-s named. She was fined 53. and cmt4 for being drunk and committed for N days for the window breaking. FURIOUS DRIVING.—William Forster was fined 55., for furiously driving his horse and trap in Flaydock on July Bth. Sergeant Bage who proved the case said that the horse was going at a veil' great rate. Qua.naELLs ABOUT CHILDREN. —Ed W:1 rd Morris was summoned on the charge of using threats at Newton on June 3rd,towards Mary Ann Harrison. The quarrel arose about the children of the complainant and defendant, and it was alleged that Morris used threats towards Mrs. Harrison. The magistrates considered the case to be a paltry one and dismissed it. FAILURE TO NOTIFY SWINE FEVE R. —Thomas Welshy, Croft, was charged with failing to notify a case of swine fever on his farm at Croft, on June 23rd. Sergeant Barnes said that he.visited the defendant's house on the above date, and found ten live pigs, four of which appeared to be suffering from swine fever. Upon the sergeant seeing Welsby, that person admitted that he bought nine pigs from a pig dealer named Heaves, one of which had died, and had been buried in the manure heap. The pig was dug up, and there were outward signs that it had died from swine fever. Superintendent Higginbottom and Inspector Kelly visited the premises soon afterwards, and reported the matter to the Board of Agriculture, who ordered their veterinary inspector, Mr. Hewitt, to make a post-mortem examination of the intestines. The inspector pronounced it to be a clear case or swine fever.—The defendant was fined 53. and costs, a:mounting in all to £1 19s. 61._

WOP.KING DURING MEAL HoURs.—MeSSTS.SMith Bros., Golborrie,were charged with employing a young person named Margaret Mitchell in a factory at Golborne, dur- ing meal hours, on the 29th June, contrary to the Fac- tory Act. They were also charged with committing a similar offence by employing Sarah Ann Pasquill dur- ing meal hours. Mr. Rowland Tinker.factory inspedtor, deposed that he visited the mill on the 28th June, at 12.56, and saw two girls, named Margaret Mitchell and Sarah A. Pasquill, cleaning the machinery. The dinner hour was from 12.30 to 1.30, and the girls ought to have been at dinner.—The girls Mitchell and Pasquill gave evidence to the effect that they were working when the inspector visited the mill. they told him that it was in accordance with the instructions of the frame-tenter, and that their dinner was ordered for one o'clorit instead of half-past twelve.—Mr, Lowe, manager, said that he had stopped the girls himself on more than one occasion from working, and told them that they were not to work during the dinner hour. The firm did not allow it, but the workpeople would work during their absence. They were fined 103. and costs in each case. A DANGEROUS PRACTICE. John Cunningham was charged with cruelty to a horse in Gelborne,on June 28. Inspector [borne, R.S.P.C.A., said that the horse in question had been blinded, and from inquiries he made, he discovered that the defendant had shot a stone from a catapult and hit the horse in the eye, with the result that it had been blinded. Mr. Stuart defended the the case. He said the Bench, in order to convict. Must be satisfied that what the defendant had done was done for the purpose of inflicting pain. He contended that there was no intention to commit cruelty at all. He was firing at a lark in the road, and the stone hit the horse. As to what part of the animal it struck they had , no evidence to show.—The magistrates decided to fine , the defendant 103., including costs. AwsAuurs.—James Williams was charged with assault- ing Thomas Tunstall, at Haydock, on July Bth. The prisoner was drunk at the time the assault took place, and was ordered out of the public-house in the occupa- tion of the brother of the complainant. A scuffle took place outside the house, during which the defendant struck the complainant. He was fined 10s.and costs.— James Bed worth was charged with assaulting Thomas Hardy, a boy about ten years of age. on 20th June. Bedworth's and Hardy's mother had quarrelled about their children, and on the above date the defendant struck the boy in the presence of his mother. The mother thereupon instituted the present proceedings. The defendant was fined 23. 6d. and costs.

AN UNVACCINATED ClTlLD.—Thomas E. Heywood', of Penketh, was summoned at the instance of Mr. Hobson, vaccination officer for the Sankey district, to showcause why an order should be made against him to have his child vaccinated.—Mr. Hobson stated that be had sent the defendant four notices requesting him to have his child vaccinated as required by law, but he declined to do so. Witness saw the defendant's wife and she told him that she did not believe in vaccination, neither did her husband, and before the child should be vaccinated they would have to he made.—The defendant stated to the magistrates that the notices which had been sent to him were under the 29'h section of the act, whereas they ought to have been under the 31st section. The Chair- man said he thought it better to adjourn the case until the next court day in order to give the defendant an op,ortnnity of having the child vaccinated. He strone,lV recommended the defendant to comply with the Act of Parliament. CHARGE AGAINST A BOAT OWNER; —,TOSepil Gordon, Liverpool, was summoned for having on the 21st ,Thne. at Sankey, allowed a canal boat to be used as a dwefiing, house without having had the same registered. M. Kerfoot, inspector of nuisances, prosecuted. The' defendant did not appear, but a person who answered the summons, stated that he was the owner of the boat, and produced certificates showing that the boat was registered. The case was adjourned in order that, the. defendant Gordon might appear. A case against Robert Flaws for using the boat as a dwelling-house was, also. adjourned.
