div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

In the House of Commons on Monday evening, Mr. ASQUITH, replying, to Mr. PICHERSGILL, said he hoped that a bill to carry out the recommendations contained in the report of the Committee on the Treatment of Habitual Drunkards would very soon be introduced in that House or in the House of Lords. Consideration of the Budget Bill as amended in Com- mittee was resumed. Sir WiTATAM littncoußT moved a new clause giving the Treasury power to remit the estate duty in respect of works of art and scientific collections left to the nation or to any county or town council. Mr. FREEMAN-MITFORIN moved an amendment to extend the scope of the new clause to any university or learned body, and Sir F. Powiar,L, in supporting the amendment, pointed to the Victoria University as a public institution deserving of the advantage of the exemption. Sir M. flicKs-BEAcia held that universities should be included. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT assented, and thus amended thenew clause was added to the bill. A new clause was added to the till, on the motion of Sir lArtm.txm HAIXOURT, giving relief in cases of joint income of husband and wife not exceeding £5OO, and at midnight the Report stage was completed and the bill ordered for third reading.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

In the House oF Commons on Tuesday evening in reply to 1`..1r. JACKS, Mr. Bank said that for many years no application had been made to the Board of Trade to use their power of taking up for traders eases of undue preference alleged against railway companies; but if any application was made it would be the duty of the Board to consider it.

ir W. HAticourwr, questioned by ??,,Tr. Donn, said he would bring in next session a bill to allow of the appoint- ment to the county bench of fit persons who were now disqua.lili4d by reason of the property qualification requirements. The right hon. gentleman stated, in raply to Sir E. A. BARTLETT,. that he had no information as.to the alleged refusal of the Argentine courts to grant the extradition of Mr. Jabez. Balfour.. The third reading of the Budget Bill was moved by Sir W. HARCOURT. Sr JOHN LUBBOCK: moved the rejec- tion of the bill. Mr. BOWLES seconded the motion. Mr. Ilott.t..ND said he found that the Budget was extremely popular. The taxation proposed. in this bill would hamper trade and throw a premium. upon foreign investments. Sir,W. THINGS-- HEARD " AND SEEN

AT WARRINGTON. It must not be a very pleasant sensation to be stranded in a strange country with scarcely a penny in one's pocket,and also without being able to speak a word of the language. This was the case with a young German in Warrington last week. Mr. Taylor, the police court missionary, had found him, and he at once took him to the Cocoa rooms, in Horsemarket-st., where he paid him his night's. lodgings,and also his breakfast for the next morning. The difficulty now was to explain this to the young German, but at length an interpreter was found, and some interesting particulars were obtained. It appeared that the German's name was Hermann Weisleder, and he had left his native land because of the conscription which compels every man in Germany to serve a portion of his life as a soldier. Hermann did not care for this, and he accordingly, ' left his native country, and became a sailor on an English steamer, which plied between Liverpool and Hamburgh. During the last week, however while he was in the Sailor's Home in Liverpool, he had all his belongings with the exception of a very small amount of money stolen from him. He then formed the intention of going to London by foot, and he was on his way when Mr. Taylor met him. In spite of his destitute circumstances. the youth- ful foreigner appeared to be quite hopeful of getting to his journey's end, although the sum total of his possessions was only 3d.

The members of the School Attendance Commit- tee do not intend to be " bossed " by the Town Council over the deputation to the ship " Clio." It will be remembered that the Committee proposed five members, who were chosen by some chance process—whether by pitch and toss, or by drawing cuts, it was not explained. The Town Council how- ever, which was in a very economic mood at its last meeting, declined to consent to the five, and ruthlessly cut the number down to three, which three being left to the Committee to decide. The Committee now refused to decide this delicate ques- tion, and have resolved that the whole of the Com- mittee shall go as a deputation. This is a reversal of the Council's decision with a vengeance, and we have perhaps not heard the last of it.

The Rev. James Bell-Cax, of St. Margaret's Church, Liverpool, who spoke at the opening cere- mony at Fairfield Schools, last week, does not attract quite so much attention as he did a few years ago, when he was so much " persecuted " for his High Church principles. Mr. Hakes has pro- bably had enough of the business, and has decided to let Mr.Bell-Cox alone. Mr. Bell-Cox having out- lived his troublous times,has for the past few years lived in comparative peace and retirement from the public gaze.

There was a very large assembly on the occasion of the opening of the new Fairfield day schools last week. The occasion was interesting, as it was the first public appearance of the Hon, John Powys, the heir of Lord Lilford, at any meeting in War- rington. lie made a distinctly favourable impres- sion, and it is to be hoped that when he has taken to himself a wife, as he shortly will do, he will be heard of more frequently in Warrington. He will have more opportunity after that interesting event has taken place, for he informed the meeting that he intended to settle dowu within easy distance of Warrington. Mr. Powys with practice will, no doubt, make a very fair speaker.

At the opening of the stillool,, almost the whole of the speakers had for their text, the threatened School Board. The Bishop of Liverpool set the ball rolling, in a letter he wrote,in which he complained of the " unreasonable demands of the Education Department." Mr. Acland is evidently not a fav- ourite with "J.C. Liverpool." The Rector spent the greater part of his speech in endeavouring to show the difference in the cost of the board and voluntary schools, much to the discredit of the former. The Rev. J. Bell-Cox was also very denun- ciatory of School Boards. The Rev. Morley Stevenson, however, did not share the gloomy apprehensions of his reverend .brothers. Ile had seen the bogey of a School Boarddangled before the ratepayers many a time, during his residence in Warrington, and the bogey had always previously been compelled" to' take a back seat." This humili- ating position would, he was confident be its fate again, and he did not fear that, Warrington would be compelled to have a School Board. With these ' pleasant assurances, the meeting was brought to a close. The schools which were opened are without doubt a credit to the committee which have had the scheme in hand, and also to the architect, and they are situated in a portion of the town where there are very few competitors.

" What another suicide 1" is getting quite a com- mon cry. Lest week there was two; one, a case of drowning and the other that of Colour- Sergeant Walsh shooting himself at Orford Barracks. The latter was an exceedingly sad case as it, showed that the deceased, who was much re- spected by his mess-mates, had made away with his life in a very determined manner. From the evidence produced at the inquest it appears that he had been ill and depressed for some time, and had at last committed suicide by fastening his toe to the trigger of a rifle and so discharging the con- tents into his head. In one of the poor fellow's pockets there was found a very pathetic letter in which he told his wife his wishes with regard to the future of his two children, and also referred to his work. The letter which was worn and frayed appeared to have been carried in the deceased's pocket for some time, and showed that he :nust have considered the fatal step before taking it. Much sympathy has been expressed with his wife by tlic officers and men of his regiment. Not only was he well liked, but he was a man, who, if he had lived, might have risen further in the service to. which he belonged,

The Cemetery Committee had no easy task in appointing a registrar for the cemetery. Their difficulties were caused not by a lack of material to seleq from but through its over-abundance. There were between sixty and seventy applicants for the post, some of them hailing from distant parts of the country. Mr. J. Taylor who has receiVed the appointment is, however, a local man and well known as he holds the honorary offices of secretary to the Workingmen's Infirmary Committee and secretary to the local Bands Association.

A very necessary improvement has now been carried out at the Central Station. I refer to the erection of an additional booking office which has been placed on the Liverpool departure platform. Messrs. Bishop and Company, borax manufacturers, some time ago pointed out to the Cheshire Lines Committee, the inconvenience to passengers caused by crossing and re-crossing of platforms in order to procure tickets, when departing for Liverpool, Southport, etc. The rail-way company have now supplied a remedy by fixing an additional office, and all that is now wanting ara the ticket racks which are expected to be ready in a short space of time. MERLIN.

div.head: 4> OPENING OF FAIRFIELD bCIIOOLS.
div.p: 4> OPENING OF FAIRFIELD bCIIOOLS.

On Thursday last week, the Fairfield schools, which have been built near Manchester-road, War- rington; were opened by the Hon. John Powys, the son of Lord Li'lord, the patron of St. Elphin's Church. The.building of the schools forms part of a scheme for the extension of school accommodation in Warrington, of which the Ellesmere-st. schools which were opened some . time ago, formed a part. It is also intended as soon as it is feasible to further extend the scheme by a rebuilding and enlargement of the Bank-st. Mission. The cost of the Fairfield schools has been £6,000, towards which a consider- able sum has been realised. The cost of the scheme has been considerably reduced by the generosity of .reland Blackburne, who has given the site, estimated to be worth £l,OOO. The archi- he present a line appearance, 'Da. Owen, and the builder, Mr. Beckett., .ord. the foundation stone was laid seven ago by Lord Cross, so that the progress of .ding had been very rapid. day of the opening,tilere was a very large ace, the large room being completely filled. Jr those present were the Rector (Rev. F. W. us), Revs. J. Beil-Cox (St. Margaret's Church, Liver- )l), Morley Stevenson, A. A. Markham, Hutt, G. B. iirston B. Percival, E. C. E. Carleton, ‘Vilcocks, H. Wild, J. J. Longhorn, and F. Slater. The Mayor , Alderman Greenall), A:deur:en Wright and Hutchinson, Councillors R. 'l'. Fairclough, and A. Woods, Messrs. W. H. J. Jenkins, H. T. Smith, W. Owen, S. limit (chief constable), and T. Morris. . After reading of prayers by the Rector, a number of letters of apology for non-attendance were read. 'lke Lord Bishop of Liverpool wrote, " Dear Mr. Willis. 1 cannot be with you on July 12, as this week it is convo- cation at York; But you must allow me to have a brick in Fairfield schools by accepting the cheque enclosed for £lO. (Applause.) I wish I could multiply it by ten times. Unhappily this year, the unreasonable demands

of the Education Department have interfered sadly with the giving. Tale my good will, good wishes, and bless- bag at the opening. Yours sincerely, J. C. Liverpool." , Mr. R. PIF.RPOINT, M.P., wrote expressing his regret that owing to hisvarliamientary duties, he was not able to be present at the opening of the schools, Mr. JOHN WHITE wrote under the date June 11th, "Dear Rector, I am requested by Lady Greenall, to write to you saying that you may put down Sir Gilbert Greenall for a donation of £2OO to the new schools at Fairfield. Lady Greenall will forward you the cheque when you require the money. Yours faithfully, J. W. White."—The Rector said that this cheque was an addition to a previous cheque for £lOO. (Applause). Mr. and Mrs. Ireland Btackburne, the Rev. J. Pulley-

bank, Mr. E. L. Phelps, and Rev. J. Willink (rector -of St., Helens), also wrote regretting their absence from the °peel ng ceremony . The RECTOR (Rev. F. W. Willis) said that he proposed to say someting concerning the report of the council of education, which had been published. The report spoke of the satisfactory increase of scholars, which it con- sidered a clue first to the increase of population,secondly to the reduction of fees, and the third cause was said to be due to the stagnation of trade. In 1870, 2,000,000 children were being taught in the day schools, now, there were 6,000,000, and the increase had been shared very fairly between Board schools. The number of voluntary schools in the country was 14,500, and the board schools numbered 5,000. The accommodation in voluntary schools was for three and a half millions, and the board schools for two millions. He would ask them to notice the difference in the cost of the two schools. In the country, the voluntary schools cost £1 17s. 61. per head, while board schools cost £2 Bs. 10. In London, however, while voluntary schools cost £2 4s. 4d. per head, the board schools cost £3 ss. Bd. He was glad to say that the voluntary contri- butions were increasing each year. He believed that while the voluntary schools were equal to the board schools in secular education, they were far superior in religious education. They had no guarantee of the religious teaching of board schools, but they had every guarantee in the church schools. They religiously set apart the first hour in the school for religious instruc- tion. A notice had recently been received from the Education Department saying that more school accom- modation would be required. A school containing 270 children had to be closed at the end of the present school year. He was thankful that they were prepared for that emergency. They knew what to do when the time arrived, and he earnestly trusted that whenever more accommodation was required, it would be supplied. He would now come to the present scheme.. They had spent upon Ellesmere-street schools £2,507 12s. 3d. Upon, Fairfield schools, exclusive of the site given by Mr. 13Iackhurne estimated to be worth £l.ooo,they had spent £5,810 9s. 7d., a total of £8,318 is. 101. They had ' received in donations 113,460 19s. id. The laying of the foundation stone had brought in £46 104. 11d. The Training College had paid them for the Mount schools £3,000. The grant to Ellesmere-street schools amounted to £l2 55., and the bank interest was £l9 13s. 2d., so that the balance still required was £1,665 18s. 2d. They owed a great deal to Mr. Ireland Blackhurne, and to the Wilson Patten family. Sir Gilbert Greenall had also been a great benefactor to them, and he thanked the Mayor especially for being present under the circum- stances which had occurred. He (the Rector) had always received great kindness from Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, ever since he had come to Warrington. He also wished to mention Mrs. Beamont. (Applause.) The amoant against Mrs. Beamont's name, did not represent what she gave, for she liked to give privately and she gave most liberally. The patron of the living, Lord Lilford, had also been most generous, and he welcomed there that afternoon his heir, the Hon. John Powys, the son of Lord Lilford, and had much pleasure in asking him to declare the schools open. (Applause.) The Hors. Jonsf POWYS said that it was with great pleasure that he received the invitation to open the schools. In so doing he was able to see more closely the place with which his family had been pleasantly associ- ated. They heard a great deal now a days of the bless- ings of education, but he asked whether any education could be really blessed, which did not teach the really true knowledge of that supreme Being upon whom their very existence depended. (Applause.) It was with this object that the present schools had been built, and it was with the greatest pleasure that he declared the schools open. (Applause.) The Rev. J. BELL-Cox next addressed the meeting at some length upon the education question. He said that he did not complain so much of the requirements of the Education Department, but he thought that more time ought to be allowed to carry them out.

The Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON next addressed the meet- in.''. He said that during the fourteen years he had been in Warrington, there had been a great number of schools built in the town. There had been St. Barnabas, Holy Trinity, Hamilton-st., Smith-st., St. James', and Riles- mere-st. schools, and now there was the Fairfield school. lie thought that that was a good evidence of what the churchmen of the town could do. He was not afraid of a School Board being established in Warrington. It had been mentioned time after time ever since he came into the town, and it was like a bogey to frighten the people, but it had always had "to take a back seat" previously, and he thought it would do the same this time. He said that there were many reasons for not having a Board School. Three of the principal reasons he thought were financial and religious reasons, and also the effici- ency of the school. After the formal ceremony was completed. Councillor A. Woods presented to the Hon, John Powys, an album containing views of the various buildings in the parish, and also an address of welcome. Mr. Woods made the presentation in one of his charac- teristically humorous speeches, and informed Mr. Powys that the parish contained 17,000 inhabit- ants. The address spoke in high terms of the generosity which Lord Lilford and his family had always displayed towards Warrington, and also congratulated Mr. Powys upois his approaching marriage, and hoped that he would often eome amongst them in the future. The address was signed by the Rev.F. W. Willis (rector), Rev.E.J. Wilcocks (head master of the Boteler Grammar School), Rev. Morley Stevenson (Principal of the Train- i'hg Colley), Mr. R. T.Fairclough (rector's warden),and Mr. A. Woods (people's warden). The views in the album were as follows :—Fairfield Schools, Warrington. Parish Church, exterior. Warrington Parish Church, in- terior, the Rectory, the Grammar Schools, National Schools, Church.st., Clergy Daughters' Schools, Training College, St. Gworge-s Mission, Bank-t. School, Riles- mere-st. School, and Smith-st. School.

The Hon. J. Powys thanked them feelingly for the present they had made him, and said that as they had mentioned his approaching marriage, he might inform them that he intended to live within easy reach of War- rington. (Applause.) He therefore hoped that they would become better acquainted with each other. The proceedings then terminated. During the even- ing the schools were open for. inspection, as also were the rectory gardens. Mr. W. S. Woods played selections upon the organ at the Parish Church during the course of the evening. The proceeds of the day amounted to £23 17s. Ocl.

NEWTON POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS, &X. Sir,—l was very pleased indeed to read the two letters in your paper of last week. I consider they very fairly represent the views of the Newton ratepayers, and I feel very grateful to the writers for writing,and you for put- ting them in the "Examiner." The Commissioaers Lave now submitted to Mr. Rich elaberate plans of a new Post Office ta be built on vacant land in connection with the Public Hall site, Earlestown. But, although Newton also required a new office, not a word has been mentioned as to their having one. The cost of the Earlestown office is estimated to be about £2,200. Mr. Rich pointed out to the Commissioners' deputation the desirability ef allowing it to stand over until next Nov- ember, when there would be a new Board, but he was assured this would not matter as there would be virtu- ally little or ng alteration in the representation. The gentlemen who told Mr. Rich this, will I think find that it is as great a mistake as the Chairman made when he stated at last monthly meeting that Mr. Smith was a Newton Commissioner. Hook forward with much hope for a very great change in the reprf sentation. In the -first place there will be five additional members. Secondly, there will be vote by ballot, and it is very doubtful if a special staff of railway clerks will be al- towed at the polling booths,but even if this be continued they will not be able to see how the men voted. The ballot is certainly a great improvement to the old sys- tem and must be a great boon to the railway workmen and others. Thirdly, some of the warns are pretty sure to send representatives not biassed to any particular interest. Fourthly, there is a general feeling that the misgovernment of the township during the last few years has been so notorious that a great effort will be - made to have new men. But the more immediate question for the ratepayers to decide is, will they allow the present Board to go in for another large building at Eaxiestown ? And it would I think be as well to remind the ratepayers what the Com- missioners have already done in this line. Take the build- ing erected at the botton end ofthe cemetery for sewerage purposes at a large cost, say some £7OO and what good have the ratepayers got from it? None ; their money has been simply squandered. Then take the building on the Market place Earlestown ; say, the cost has been another £7OO. What useful purpose dees this serve the ratepayers to day? Simply a -white elephant. It is• neither being used for men nor beast. Then there is the more recent " job " the Public Hall with ',which we are so familiar. Seeing their failure has been so greal; in public buildings it seems to be vet y undesirable to allow them to go in for a new Post office. Instead of the cost being£2,2oo as estimated do not be surprised if it reach £4.400. Our experience is that they are the right men to manipulate the cost in this way, The Public Hall cost far more that double what it originally was intended Then what do the Newton ratepayers gain by this out- lay at Earlestown. Are the ultimately to have a post office at Newton as well? Not if the present commis- sioners can prevent it. They will simply have the privi- lege of paying the same as they do for the Public Hall and without any return whatever. It remains to be seen if Newton will be quiescent or rise up as one man and stop another job being perpetrated by the prese.nt (almost defunct) Commissioners. I should like to see the Newton people rise to the occasion and attend the public meeting which will be held in the Newton Ward at an early date, and protest against the latest action of the Newton Board of Corn- missioners,—l am, yours respectfully, AIIOTHER NEWTON RATEPAYER. Newton July 19th 1894.

div.head: DEATH OF ALDERMAN ASHTON.
div.p: DEATH OF ALDERMAN ASHTON.

On Saturday evening, at about 845, Alderman !'Ashton passed away at his residence, the Bridge 'lnn, Latchford. The deceased gentleman, who had attained the age of 78 years, had only been ill for shout a week, from an attack of bronchitis. Be was attended during his illness by Dr. White, and Dr. T. Starkey Smith. Alderman Ashton was born at Thatto Heath, St. Helens, and for a great number of years was a guard on the L. & N.W. Hallway, afterwards becoming stationmaster at Arpley station, Ire subsequently entered into the ranks of the licensed victuallers, taking the Bridge Inn, which he occupied to the time of his death. He entered the Town Council for the Latchford Ward in 1872, and at each successive election up to 1893, he has been re-elected. In that year he was elected to fill an aldermanic vacancy in the Council, and it wagon this election that the memorable scene in which Councillor Roberts P7A3 so prominent an actor took place. Alderman Ashton was the vice-chair- man of the Cemetery Committre.and was also a member of the Paving and Sewera;e, Markets, Fire Enc,,ine. and General Purposes Committees. He had been married three times, and had 29 children, ten of whom, eight sons, and two daughters, survive him.

THE FUNERAL. 1 The funeral took place on Wednesday at noon. The kearse and funeral coaches left the deceased alderman's residence at 11-30. The coaches were preceded by tut members of the police force in command of Inspector Bowen, after which followed twelve members of the fire brigade under the supervision of Superintendent Turner. Then came a coach in which were the Mayor. (Alder- man Graenall), and the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle). Several coaches containing members of the Town Council and Licensed Victuallers' Association preceded the hearse. On each side of the hearse • were four guards from the L.Br, N.W. Railway,whn acted as bearers, and were under the supervision of Mr. Starkey, the stationmaster of Bank Quay Station. The blinds of the windows of the public houses on the .route to the cemetery were drawn, in respf•cr, to the deceased. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. F. Slater, and the following members of the Warrington Corporation were present: The Mayer, Aldermen Francomb, Harrison. Sutton, and Hutchinson ; Councillors Muir, Hdl, Smethurst, Longton, and ' Bennett; Messrs J. Lyon Whittle, ( Town Clerk), T. Longdin (Borough Surveyor),and Taylor (Gas Manager). Messrs Holbrook and Hayes were present, representin the Conservative Association, and Messrs Leather and Ripley represented the Wildersnool Brewery. The fol- lowing members of the Licensed Victuallers" Association were present : Messrs J. Evans ( president ), Peers Brimelow (secretary), Turley, Sampson, Allison, Wright, Kershaw, James. J. Boardman, W. Ostler. J. William- Son, Lake. and Lea. The eight bearers were Guards Bolton, Limb, Williamson, Curry, Smalley. Newton, Burke, and Ratcliffe. The procession from the chapel to the family vault was preceded by the members of the family, and Messrs Yarwood, J. Lnwis. and P. Chrimes • (brothers-in-law). Wm. Ashton(brother), Ripley,L-ather, Hill. Gownlockc, Britch. Lambert, Bramhall, and J. Taylor (Lion Hotel). A large number of wreath.; were sent. The funeral arrangements were in the hands of Mr. Peter Chrimes, who gave every satisfaction.

div.head: LATF, Silt GILBERT GREENALL
div.p: THE LATF, Silt GILBERT GREENALL
BART.

The Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis) en Sunday even- ing alluded to the death of the late t_sir Gilbert - Greenall. Bart., during the course of his sermon at the Parish Church. He based his r,warks upon the Ist Chronicles 29c. 28v. "And he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour, and Solomon his son reigned in his stead." He said that he had been much struck with what he I.aff heard of Sir Gilbert Greenall's firm adherence through tile to those political principles which he beliavr d to be right. Ile never wavered from those principles. althou2h he might see ,reason to modify them from time to time, as life went on. He was always consistent in regard to what he believed to be right and true. He (the Rector), th.ught that Sir Gilbert was deserving of a passing notice, when they considered that he had been representative of War- rington for 35 years, and his poll, icat life had extended over half a century. He had been wise and generous in the use of the money whieh God had Liven him. They , all knew how liberally and wisely lie had used that money and how he had helped the work of the church in this town, and how he was always ready to assist educa- tion, assist missions and hoFpitals, and relieve the dis- tressed. He had a shrewd judgment aid was not (vigil% imposed upo7:. He (the Rector) hoped that Sir Gilbert's son would be a wise man and a good man, and that he 'might be a bles7,ing to all with whim lie. catne in contact. --AX the close of the service, the organist, Mr. W. S. Weoda, played the Dead March in Saul.
BANKRUPTCY OF A RUNCORN GROCER.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court yesterday (Friday) before Mr. Registrar Ridgway, John Stringer, grocer, Runcorn, came up to undergo his public examination by Mr. A. B. Potter, the assistant official receiver. The bankrupt stated that he commenced ' business in 1869, as a Scotch travelling draper in War- rington without capital,and gave up that business about twelve years ago, when he commenced the grocery business with a surplus over his liabilities of £lO. Ile had been previously in partnership with David Miller in the Scotch drapery business but had dis- solved partnership with him. In 1871, his liabilities weie £3,000, and assets £2,000, but he had been able to clear off his liabilities. This was the first occasion on which he had ever been bankrupt. He attributed his insolvency to loss of 18 houses which had been con- demned as insanitary by the Runcorn Commissioners. The tenants of these houses had also been customers of his. His loss from that transaction had been £2OO. He was first aware of his insolvency in November, when he lost the houses, and had since contracted debts of between £2O and £4O. He thought :it possible that he might pull through or he Wopld not have con- tracted those debts, otherwise he had no justification for so doing. The property had been left him by his father. He got no compensation when the houses were closed. His total liabilities were £399, and assets £9 7s.—Mr. Potter said that as far as he was con- cerned, the examination might close that day, and the , registrar therefore made an order to that effect subject to the signing of the notes of evidence.

div.head: " EAUR OWD FISHERMON ! "
div.p: " EAUR OWD FISHERMON ! "

Wen a jolly owd joker i' Nyowton— A rale deawnreet, genooin' sort,— Wo con byet aw fro here to Bowton At fishin', his favorite sport. Its a seet fer sore e'en, when he's watchin' For wrigglin's at th' eend o' his rod : An' he's switherin' wot he'll be catchin'— A dace, er a pike, er a Cod ! " Sammul " sez he knows every crater That swims i' that dear owd bruck, An' he's saran' that, sooner er later, owd sportsmon u'il hey um—wi' luck! Wen he's gettm' him ready fer action, Yo don't hear him whistle er sheaut ; But he chuckles wi' greyt satisfaction, At th' thowts o' a dinner o' treaut ! Wen he goes to his work i' a mornin', His button hole's railly a see t ; But a fishin' rod's moor his adornin', Wen he's off fer a journey at neet. " Sammul " sez he's weel woth eaur attention, (But this may he only a tale!) For he's sure ther's no fish yo con mention, He mum% catch, fro a srimp to a whale! He knows wheer the big'st on um lodges, An' he reads aw ther ways like a book ; Wile a pike may be up to his dodges, He's noan so lung " takkin' his hook !" "Well, well, owd lad, lung may thi fishin' Be followed bi nowt but good luck ; But we hope an' we pray, an' we're wis'ain' Theau'l mind an' not tumble 'ith bruck "Get Sammul 'to see that his Booard Is safe fer a tidy sized Mon; Or eaur grief fer aw time is assur'd— We'st ne'er smile agen wen theaur't gone! "We don't want a Crunner deaun here, Ner jury to tell heaw theau deed ; Fer a verdict wad read rayther queer, "Accidental, through catchin' a feed !' " "So, mind, my owd friend, wot theaur't doin'— We don't want to Berry thi yet; An' we'd rayther thi chums war not raein', Throo seem' thi lodgins' "To Let "Good Lord! if owt happens thi welfare, We's't aw sup cowd sorrow to th' dregs; An' taste heaw the sad 'uns i' hell fare— Yore's, swattin' wi' frest— O'PEGS. Rose Bonk, 27, 4, '94.
NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Just now the temperance question in Earlestown appears to be one of the topics about which men are beginning to think very seriowsly, insomuch that nothing will satisfy them but. that they must join some teetotal organisation or other. What has caused thi.:3 I am not in a position to say, but some iew trninths ago I was afraid the Good Templar? were about to suffer somewhat from some little disagreement which ended in dissension. Of course, to some eNtent, the parent lodge Was rather crip- pled, and the offshoot had great expectations. Now I am told, however, that the parent lodge has re- covered its position, and is flrollin,g members in large numbers. The present position of the lodge is phenomenal, ana has not been equalled during the term of its existence. The members are in high jinks, and they expect shortly to hale a centenary celebration. I don't know whether tile other lodge holds as good a position, but I hardly see how two lodges are to be .kept going with any great measure of success.

Inspector Kelly is leaving the neighbourhood,nr/d though he is not seeking fresh fields and pasturel new, still he is going to take up a position to which is attached much tfreater responsibility than apper- tains to his position here. He goes to Leig,h,whictr is the, place from whence he came,thongh in altered Circumstances, and I have no doubt, the Leigh people will be as pleased to see MOW we are sorry to lose him. Mr. Kelly has only been in this neigh- bourhood about two years, but during that time h. 3 has found his way into the esteem and respect of the townspeople. We do not know who his suc- cessor may be, but we know this much, that Mr. 'Kelly has by his courtesy made it difEcult for another to follow.

div.p: ST. HELENS.
WIFE ASSkITZT.

A young fellow named James Tucker,. of Waver-Ft., was charged at St. Helens. on Monday, with an a,gra- vated assault ri-pcn his wife by severely beating and kicking her because she liad previously summoned hiu brother for threats. Complainant said her husband had thrashed her nearly every day since she was married.. Defendant's story was that his wile was the aggressor.— The magistrates adjourned th:J case for a week for a settlement.

div.head: ACCIDENTS.
div.p: ACCIDENTS.

At two on Monday afternoon, Sohmon Williams, a middle-aged labourer, Hardy-st., St. Helens, fell clown the hoist in the Jubilee Warehouse, Illkinaton's Sheet Glass works. He was taken to Proyidenc? Hospital with a broken right thigh.—On Saturday night:nom:is M`Queeny, aged fifty. of St. John-st.,was; firing furnaces attached to the salt cake revolving plant at Greenbank Chemical Works, when the flames burst out, and he was badly burned on the face and hands.

div.head: PIZSTILFGES OF PUBLIC LIDUARIES,
div.p: THE PIZSTILFGES OF PUBLIC LIDUARIES,

At the meeting of the St. Helens Free Public Libraries Committee on Wednesday, a resolution was carried that the rules and regulations as to the lending libraries should be altered so as to provide as follows :—Borrowers shall he of two classes—viz.,persons being ratepayers or resident within the borough shall be entitled to become borrowers without any payment, and persons not being ratepayers or resident, but employed in the borough, shall he entitled to bec.,,me borrowers on payment of an annual subscription of 53.

div.head: LLEGF.D EBIBEZZ LP:3I ENT.
div.p: A LLEGF.D EBIBEZZ LP:3I ENT.

At the St. Helens Police Court on Monday, before Messrs. Walmesley-Cotham, and II Martin, Henry J. Egginton, of Greenfield-road, St. Helens, was charged with omblezzling ss. 6,1., the property of John Ashley. Mr. H. L. Riley, who prosecute,'" stated that the defend- ant was employed as a collector by Ashley, who was the 10-2:41 representative of Mr. Waddilove, trading as the Providea Clothing Club. Defendant was charged with having received three small sums of money, aryl mis- appropriating them in a manner rendering him liable to the penalty for embezzlement. Defendant's books showed a total deficiency ot ..9.20 or £3O, and his excuse at the time was the losses of the coal strike ; but as a matter el fact the sums had been misappropriated since the coal strike.—Mr. J. P. ;Warns, for the defence, con- tended that as Mr.Waddilove was defendant's employer, and al that name was entered in the agreement, he should he the prosecutoe.—Th, Mag,istrate's Clerk said anyone could prosecute for a felony.—John Ashley, the prosecutor, sta`ed that la, wer:t the round of the cos- tomers, and from what he discovered had an interview • with the defendant at the office. The total deficienchs he found come to £22 ss. 3d., which included the three sums mentioned in the information. Defendant, said lie ' had to take the money to live on. His salary was 75.6 d. a week, in addition to c,mmission, which was 7A per cent. In an ordinary way defendant could earn 30a to 355. a week, but tie c.,ithi llt sav that any local collector was at the present earning that. On several occasions defendant had m tt'.e. more tan 15s. a week, but had never made £1 it week since the strike.—Mr. Mearns, for the d9lenee, eootended that time matter was a mere question of accounts, that sheuld be settled in a.civil court, and alSo that the offence had been con. doned.—Th, bench tined the defendant £s,or twenty-one days imprisonment.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JULY 21, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JULY 21, 1894.
NoTEs ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.

CRICKET. The Warrington team took the opportunity on Saturday of having their revenge upon Wigan fora defeat which that team had inflicted upon thEm a few weeks ago. They were without S. M Crosfield and E. Connor, but they nevertheless were equal to the task of disposing of the Wiganers pretty easily. One of the largest 1 " gates " of the season was present to witness the match, which showed that the interest in the cricket team has not diminished to any appreciable extent, notwithstand- ing the numerous defeats which the Warringtonians have suffered. The Wigan captain won the toss and decided to bat first. There were several very good scores made by the visitors, the highest being Goodwin with 45. Knowles, Littlewood, and Barnwell also made 24, 20, and 17 respectively. Clark kept the wicket so well, and the Warrington fielding was so good, V:,.at although the Wigan total was 145, only two extras were given, one of them teing a wide by Bates. Four bowlers were tried during the Wigan innings, and each of them proved fruitful in the way of wickets. Wordsworth had the best analysis with two for 14. R. Smith was shghtly worse with three for 29. The other two bowlers, J. J. Crosneld, and Bates. were not quite so successful.

Warrington had only —"a 1-i-;:tle more than an licur and a 1 haif to wipe off the Wigan score, but they scored so rapidly that 153, eight runs ahead, were scored for the loss of only five wickets, before time was called. Bates and Mortimer, the first two batsmen each made the same score 45, there being three scores of 45 in the match. Wordsworth was the only player to fail to attain double figures. The winning hit of the match was made by R. Smith a little before time, and this was hailed with loud cheers by those present. The only successful Wigan bowler was Leigh-Clare who captured three wickets for 25 runs.

The Warrington team meet Northern to-day, at Arpley. Judging from the match, the Warrington team should be again successful. It will be remembered that at Liverpool, at the first meeting of the teams, Warrington had very hard lines indeed in n&t winning the match, as they had almost reached their opponents' score when they were robbed of victory by the arrival of the time for finishing the match. The prospect of seeing another good match should attract a good"gate," providing Jupiter Pluvius withholds his plentiful supplies of rain. --- Tne Sankey Wesleyans journeyed to Winsford on Saturday, to antagonise the Wharton Parish Church. This was the second meeting of the two teams' and like the first, it resulted in an easy win for the Warring- tonians. Booth " pleed " very well for his 21, but received a severe blow in the head durinc, the operation. The other double figure men on the Sankey Bridges side were Peers 18, Taylor and Hardy 12, and Bailey 10. ' Watkins worked havoc amongst the Whartonian wickets, fer he secured seven out of the ten ,five of these being clean bowled. Jefferson kept wicket very well, and only one extra was recorded by the homesters. The only player among the saltmen to do anything was Southworth,who was very lucky in securing 24 runs out of the 44 which were scored en his side.

The Sankey Wire Mills gained an excellent victory on Saturday at the expense of Weston. This was due in a great measure to the excellent batting of Marshall who compiled 45 runs before Kershaw found the way to his wicket. Cook, the wicket keeper, also played an excel- lent game, for he scored 16 not out. The Wire Mills innings realised the satisfactory total of 102, to which the opposing team replied with 73. The Tudors were not quite so plentiful in the Weston team as usual,there being only two. In some of the matches, it would be almost correct to style the Weston team, the Team of Tudors. There are not many junior teams who can boast of lowering the Westonians' colours, so that the Wire Mills are to be complimented upon their performance on

Saturday. The St. Mary's team had an easy task on Saturday in disposing of the Y.M.C.A. Not one of the latter obtained double figures while Pickton alone, for the St. Mary's scored 34, only six below the Y.M.C.A. total. Bates bowling waa way guccessful, for he captured seven of the" young an'" wicke

The Cheshire Lines Engineers overwhelmingly defeated Winwick on Saturday, for while WinwiO4 pnlvcrd 16, of which l c?3le OEIO, ne Engineedpiled ori 125, I\lookii bowiltij atrage was Less than a run per wicket, for he obtained six wickets for five runs, and then not satisfied with this he went in first of his side with the bat, and scored 27, the highest score of the match. Lawless was not far behind him however, for he made 26. The other respectable scorers were Robin- son, 22, and Hackett 17.

Among the other junior matches, Cairts-StfeEtt Unity beat the Amateurs by 59 to 37. Monks, Bennett and Knowles were mainly responsible for this result. The Arpley Juniors through the instrumentality of Houghton and Whitehe ad, inflicted a crushing defeat upon Man- chester-road second. Buckley-street were too good for the St. Anne's, Gibion's bowling being unusAally des- , trufztive, for he took eight wickets for four runs,

ILancashire gained a SetiSationai victofY (Wei Portiettet on Tuesday, as they commenced and finished the Match in one dsy. This feat is a very rare one, the last titnc It was performed being in 1892, when curious to say, tho same two teams operated on the same ground at Old Traffor3, and LaOcabire alss on that time came out the winners. The heroes of the match on Tuesday were Mold and Sugg, the onq with the ball and the other with the bat. Mold was simply unplayable, for in the first innings, which by the way wore alnacst the smallest of the present season, he took seven wickets for ten runs, , performed the " hat trick once, and tor* three more Wicket's in four balls. In the second innings he took seven for 55. ThEv performanc2 of Mold quite overshadowed Briggs whs tAbk three for 15, a very good record if it stood by itsalf.• Sup.,g had done very little this season previous to Tugtda.y, hut on that day (ma very slow wicket, he scored•lo6in an hour and twenty minutes. This victory which is the second for Lancashinin the cmunty tourna- ment this season was a very dec:Aive one for whereas they stOred- 257;,, Somerset only scored 31 and 123.

div.head: BowuNo.
div.p: BowuNo.

Latf Saturday the members of the ITaninton Liberal Club bowling team had, what turned out to be the ,pleasantest outing of the season. BeclforaLeigh was th,. team chogen to be " licked,' but they, it 3eerfl9, had a different opinion on the matter for they turned round and " licked the lickers." For the last few weeks the Warrin7ton team have had a run of had luck that has been sufficient to damp•the spirits of most people, but not of the Warrington men. Sorely a way can be- Sound to turn the scale. The. teams were very strong at this match numbering, no fewer than 18 a side and 13 points were fixed as the limit of the gatne. Fifteen Bedford Leigh men scored the full number whilst only three of the Warringtonians were able to do the same. The journey to Bedfoid Leigh was made by 'buses through an exceedingly pleasant part of the country in very tine weather. The distance is 11 miles and was covered in a little over an hour.. After the match the " bowlers" partook of an excellent tea, 'provided by the landlord of the Bowling Green Hotel, Leigh, during which several toasts were proposed and accepted. The journey home was commenced at nine o'cliack, Warrington being reached a little after ten.

The semi-final of the Lancashire and Cheshire Bowling Association took place at the Leigh Bowling Green on Saturdav,the two clubs being Bull's Head,Warrinton,,S. and klinCisford. The match was a most exciting one, and resulted in a win for Hindsford hy 216' to 215. The Hindsford men were seven bAind with only two men to play, but these two men gained the necessary points and thus won by one point. The evenness of the scoring is well shown by the fact that six on each side scored 22. The worst beating in the match was that of of Warrington, who only scored four to his opponent 21.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

The ‘Varrington Cycling Club members formed then - selves into two groups on Saturday, one party to the number of twenty proceeding to Winnington to witness the sports which were being held there, and the other half of the club went as far as Arley and Plunihlev, the place appointed on the fixture card. At the Winnington sports a member of the club, A. T. Daintith,distinguished himself by his excellent riding. In the half-mile rare he carried off the first prize, which was a handsome walnut bookcase and chetfioneer, valued at ,c 21.0. Fie was. also successful in the one mile race, securing the seco.n d prize which consisted of a set of cutlery.

div.head: SWIMMING.
div.p: SWIMMING.

A few days ago there was rather an excitim, incident in the new Warrington plunge bath. A young man who works at a farm at Winwick was observed to he strine- gling in the deep end of the bath. 'The unfortunate youth had gone down twice before it occurred to anyone that he was drowning. When this was discovered a boy who was standing on the side ran to fetch the bath.- keeper, Mr. Barlow. Mr. Barlow at once saw the criti- cal position of the bather and plunged in with his clothes on and succeeded in rescuing the youth just a. he was about to sink for the last thee. Mr. Barlow is to he con- gratulated on the prompt manner in which he sprana to the help of the drowning bather. Wo urderstand that there are life-belts and an el.,e,tric communication from !he bath to Mr. Barlow's offico, provid.d for such emer- gencies as these. but in the confusion of the moment they were probably forgotten.

School work commenced at the above schools on Monday. The number of children on the books in the various departments is as follows :—Upper girls, mistress Miss Norman, 115; lower girls, mistress Mrs. Stans.field, 320; infants, mistress Miss Shaw, 290.

div.head: P.S.A. AT THE Y.M.C.A.
div.p: P.S.A. AT THE Y.M.C.A.

On Sunday the above meeting was presided over by Mr. T. S. Kent. An earnest and impressive address on prayer was delivered by Mr. W. H. Bayley. Two solos were rendered in a pleasing manner by Mr. A. Baker, viz :—" The Haven,' and "Die voice of Jesus." A second batch of prizes was distributed by the chairman to members who had made the requisite number of attendances. Mr. 11. Page and Mr. Gregson also took part in the , meeting.

div.head: LOCAL ATHLETES AT WINNINGTON.
div.p: LOCAL ATHLETES AT WINNINGTON.

At the annual sports held at Winnington Park, Northwich, on Saturday, J. Fair, Warrington, secured second place in the quarter mile handicap, with 3'2 yards start. In the half mile bicycle race A. T. Daintith, Warrington, from the 75 yards mark, came in first, and also gained second place in the mile bicycle race.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOYS AT SOUTHPORT.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOYS AT SOUTHPORT.

30 more poor boys w!.io had been selected by Mr. Riley and Mr. Jones, school attendance officers, left Warrington on Monday for a week's encampment at Southport. This makes a total of nearly 90 boys from Warrington who have spent a week under canvas, and have derived considerable benefit as well as pleasure from the change of air and scenery. SE-WING MACHINES, Hand £2 18s. 6d. Treadle £4 4s. wi. h handsome walnut cover.—J. and W. DUTTON, 16 and 1 d Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt. THE RIVER DREDGING.

The dredging of the river at Warrington not hav- ing been finished by June, the Ship Canal Company are now incurring a penalty of £5O a day. It is said, however, that the company have asked for a modification of the penalty, and the Corporation are considering the matter. No doubt when the work has been completed a considerable abatement will be made. A great deal of interest is taken in the dredging operations as will be seen from the crowds which are always congregated near to where the dredgin‘:,i is taking place. Nit. Wm. PIERPOINT, J.P., IN LONDON.
A dinner was given on Wednesday evening at the National Liberal Club, London,by the Liberal mem- bers of Parliament of Lancashire,to the Right Hon. _ _ _ _

J. Bryce. the President of the Board of Trii.de, and late Chancellor of the Duchy, and Lord Tweeddale, the present chancellor. A number of representatives from various Liberal associations of Lancashire were present. and the Warrington Association was reprPsepted by Mr.Wm.Pierpomt,J.P. At the dinner interesting speeches were given by the guests of the evening and various Members of Parliament upon the political questions of the day.

div.head: CHRISTIAN POLICE ASSOCIATION.
div.p: CHRISTIAN POLICE ASSOCIATION.

On Wednesday afternoon, by the kind invitation of Miss B. Dutton, the wives of the members of the Warringtonian Christian Police Association were entertained at the Willows, Moore. A splendid tea was partaken of, after which the party dispersed for walks in the neighbourhood. Later in the even- ing several games were enjoyed on the lawn. The afternoon's proceedings were brought to a close by a supper, after which the party returned home well pleased with their outing, and with the kindness of Miss Dutton.

A TRIP TO SOUTHPORT. The choir and churchwardens of All Saints' Mission, Bewsey-road, accompanied by the clergy, had their annual trip to Southport, oa Monday. A Start was made at half-past-nine, and on arriving at the favourite health resort, the party dispersed and spent the day in Tisiting the various places of int;clt, the rieW Marine lakes claiming their share. div.head: LOCAL VETO-AN INGENIOUS PLACARD.
div.p: LOCAL VETO-AN INGENIOUS PLACARD.

Visitors to tho agricultural shows during the present season will probably (says the "Leeds Mercury") have their attention drawn to a bill which is evidently meant for general circulation. The following is a copy of the. bill, which one of our reporters brought from the Lin- colnshire stow, held at Grimsby. It is printed by a London firm, but bears no other mark of its origin. Per- haps none is needed. Here it is : Important—To visitors to the show—lf the threatened Veto Bib were law and adopted here, no alcoholic liquor could have been sold in the show ground. Only hotels would be allowed to supply any drink, and then only to those who had taken beds or were having their Meals. What would have been the result? Many would have been inconvenienced. The show would never in future be held in a Veof town.

THE MINIMUM WAGE.

meeting of the Coal Trade Conciliation Bard was held in London on Thursday. It was announced last evening that it had been res,)lved that the present rate of wages should be reduced from the Ist August by tak- ing off the !aFt two advances of 5 per cent. each, and that the w,trps shall remain at that rate until the Ist January, /896. Resolutions were also adopted establish- ing a minimum rate of wages, as proposed, for two years, and probably that the Board of Conciliation should be continued for two years.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this board was held on Thursday Afternoon in the Board room, Daresbury. The chair was occupied by Mr. S. Burgess,and there were also present Messrs. Darbyshire, Parr, Darlington, John- son, Tickle, Bradford, Aaron, Beswick, Hall, Rout- ledge, Maddock, Moore, Major Fox, Mr. Linaker (clerk), and Mr. Swinton (surveyor).

div.head: PAYMENT FOR TEAM LABOUR.
div.p: THE PAYMENT FOR TEAM LABOUR.

Mr. Aaron, in accordance with notice given, moved that the price to be paid in future for team labour be 14s. per day for a pair of horses and man, and Bs. per day for one horse and man. In moving his motion Mr. Aaron contended that the present prices paid, namely 12s. and 7s. respectively, were insufficient, seeing that farmers had now to pay 3s. 6d. per day for manual labour.—Mr. Tickle seconded the motion, and said the Board had great difficulty in getting carting done at the present prices.—Mr. Parr contended that the *present prices were satisfactory.—Mr. Hall also objected to in- creasing the price and pointed out that the Corporation of -Warrington w ere able to get a horse and man for ss. 10d. per day.—Mr. Johnson said the present prices had been given for about 30 years. Then they could get a man for about 10s. per week, but now they had to pay 183. and 20s. per week.—At the present prices it did not pay farmers to do the carting.—Mr. Darlington thought the present a fair price. On being put tG the vote Mr. Aaron's motion was lost by two votes.

div.head: NUISANCE AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: A NUISANCE AT LATCHFORD.

Mr. Frank W. Kerfoot, nuisance inspector for the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority, wrote to the Board stating that a nuisance existed in Ackers's-lane, Latchford, by the offensive smell from drains caused by several entrapped gullies. He asked the Board to remedy the defect, or proceedings would be taken against them. It was decided on the motion of Mr. Hall, seconded by Mr. Bradford, that the Surveyor be instructed to stop the nuisance. THE BOARD AND THE CANAL.-STRONG COMPLAINTS. The Board's Ship Canal Committee in their report to the board stated that they had visited several bridges across the Runcorn and Latchford canal, and found them in a very dangerous condition. The Manchester Ship Canal Company who -aeria responsible for them, were doing nothing to put them in proper order. They also reported that they found that the Canal Company had laid a double set of rails along the Runcorn and Latchford canal without asking the Committee's permission to do so. The Consmittee further stated that the Canal Com- pany had failed to carry out several of the agreements with the board, and the committee requested the board to terminate all av,reements between the Canal Company and the board. The committees minutes were passed on the proposition of Mr. Aaron seconded by Mr. Moore.— The Chairman said that the Canal Company would

premise anything and do nothing. They had not carried out half of the agreements which they had made with that board, and which Sir Leader Williams promised should be carried out when he met the board's Ship Canal Committee. The Clerk said the company had had plenty of time to carry out the work since the committee met them in April. The agreements were then read, and the Surveyor reported which had been carried out. It was found that the company had fulfilled eight agree- ments, and left undone nine.—Mr. Hall said the Canal Company had done the least important ones,—Mr. Darbyshire was of the opinion that the board had been I too lax with the Canal Company and thought they should "stick more closely to them." He referred to several inconveniences to the public caused by the non-carrying out by the Canal Company of their agreements. Mr. Parr also spoke of the unfair treatment the board at re- ceived at the hands ef the Canal Company.—Mr. Hall proposed the following resolution "That the Ship Canal Company not having carried out the undertakings with the board, the Clerk be authorised to serve formal notice on the Canal Company terminating with them all agree- ments with the board, within seven days, in accordance L with the agreement." Mr. Parr seconded the resolution, I and it was carried unanimously. THE RIGHT OF WAY AT LATCHFORD LOCKS. Mr. Burgess said he understood that the Canal Com- pany had prevented people from crossing the canal at Latchford Locks. It stated very distinctly in a section of the Ship Canal Act, that a good foot-road, with suit- able hand-rails, free from all charge, was to he placed at or near to Latchford Locks. He had been under the impression that the Canal Company intended to allow the public to cross at the locks. It was decided to com- municate with the canal company asking them whether the road. Was to be across the locks. FINANCE. The Finance Committee reported that the balance in hand was £743 is. 9d. Four townships Had not yet paid up their calls, viz :—Hatton, Latchford, Halton and Psrtington. This was all the business of public interest.

ANNIvP.RSARY SERVICES AND CHILDREN'S- TnEmr„—The anniversary services in connection with the Primitive Methodist School, Frodsham,were conducted on Sunday morning and evening, in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, large congregations attending each. div.head: ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT.

WEDNESDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Shand. THE FARMER AND HIS ELECTRICAL INCUBATOR.—The Anells Electrical Engineering Company sued Robert Pownall, farmer, of Sutton, St. Helens, for £2 17s. 6d. in respect of an clectrial appliance supplied to him. Mr. Abell said time defendant broaght an incubator to him and asked him if he could invent an electric arrange- ment to regulate the heat. Witness experimented, and ultimately produced a machine, which worked well. Defendant then took a farm at Sutton, and laid out a plan for breeding fowls on a large scale by his incuba- tors. the instrument made was a perfect one, and worked properly.—Defendant said the instrument was worthless, and produced it in court. He placed 600 eggs .in the incubator, and the arrangement worked all right for a time. It failed to regulate the heat, and the whole of the eggs were roasted.—lt transpired that the plain- tiff company were in liquidation.—His Honour said that the action should have been taken by the liquidator, and he non-suited the plaintiffs with costs. IMPORTANT TITHE CASIL—The Provost and Scholars of King's College, Cambridge, brou9ht an action against the trustees of the Society of Friends, St. Helens, for £2 12s. 101. for rectorial tithes due from land in St. Helens, of which the defendants were owners. Canon Mitchell, of Prescot, also sued the trustees in respect of £2 6. 9 1., vicarial tithe. Dr. W. J. Sparrow (instrurted by Mr. F. Smith) appeared for the plaintiffs in the first , case, and Mr. Charlton, of Manchester, defended. Dr. Sparrow said the application was under sub-section 3 of section 2 of the Tithes Aet, 1891. for the appointment of a receiver. The trustees were the owners of land in the heart of st. Helens, and it was a pure question, so far as he knew, for his honour's decision.—Mr. Charlton argued that the lessees of the land were the persons who should pay the tithe rent. The trustees had granted building leases on portions of the estare for terms of 999 years, and were nAw receiving a yearly rent, which was all the interest they had in the land. He submitted that the person intended by the Act to be liable was lie who held the land from the trustees, and was the landlord, lessor, or owner of the buildings which was erected by -him,and occupied by tenants of itis.—Dr. Sparrow said a careful reading of the clause would knock the bottom out of everything Mr. Charlton had said.—A long legal argu, moot followed, and his Honour intimated that he would re ser vejudgment. •

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons, on Thursday, Mr. H.GARD- NER, replying to suggestions by Mr. FIELD that foreign cattle landed at the Woodside and Wallasey lairages in the port of Liverpool had been subjected to injurious treatment through the want of a sufficient reception lairage, stated that inquiries were being made. Mr. GARDENER informed MT. T. E. ELLIS that there was no favourable prospect at present of his being able to dis- pense with the normal statutory requirement of slaughter at the port of landing in the case 'of cattle im- ported from Canada. Sir M. HICKS BEACH obtained leave to move the adjournment in order to call attention to the CHANCULLOR of the EXCHEQUER'S, statement on public business during the remainder of the session. Sir M. HICKS 13macnargued in considerable detail that the work enumerated in that statement could not be performed, adding that Sir WM. HARCOURT was not fulfilling his promise to allow fair time for discussion of Supply. Sir WMi HARcounT defended his views as to the possibility of accomplishing the work, and said that ten days more should be enough for Supply. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN dwelt on the need for adequate time ta discuss Supply. Sir M. Hteus BEACH'S motion for the adjournment was rejected by a majority of 51. _ _ .

Mr. JOHN MORLEY moved the aecond, reading of the Evicted Tenants Bill. Colonel SAIINDERSON moved and Mr. W. KENNY seconded a motion that it should be con- sidered that day six months. After several other mem- bers had spoken, the debate was adjourned.

In the House of Lords, the Parochial Electors (Regis- tration Acceleration) Bill was read a second time. The Sea Fisheries (Shell Fish) Bill and. the Locomotive (Threshing Engines) 818 were read a third time, and passed. The Zanzibar Indemnity Bill was read a second time. The report from the Select C'ommittee on the principle of betterment as applied to•town improvements was adopted after some discussion. The Finance Bill was brought from the Commons. and Lord Seim- RIMY, having regard to the difficulty of master- ing the details of the measure, asked that the second readinc, might not be taken before that day week. Lord ROSEBERX did not think it neces- sary that they should master the details, because he did not admit that their lordships had anything to do with the measure. Lord SALISBURY' asserted that there was a precedent for the House of Lords discussing a Finance Bill and dividing upon it, but admitted that as long as the House of Commons adhered to the view that it would not accept amendments introclnced by the Lords in Money Bills, it was of course useless to make them. The Bill was read the first time, and the second reading was fixed for Thursday.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT MEDICAL AND SURGICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT MEDICAL AND SURGICAL SOCIETY.

A meetinz of this society was held last week at the 'depOt when there were present the Rev; 3 Car- son, J. Allatt, E. W. W. Kaye, Drs. Mounzey, and Valentines Mr. Dring, and the secretary (Mr. A. Peake). Letters of apology were received from the Revs. H. Monk and F. 3. Lennon. The Rev. J. Carson presided. The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed. The, secretary re- ported that collections had been made at the various works in the district, resulting as follows—Viaduct Works £lO is. 3d., Vulcan Foundry, £B, 16s. 101., Mc- Corquodale and Co.'s works, £2 7s, ad., C. B. F. Borron and Co. £1 12s. Subscriptions .—Mrs. Jones 55., Mr. Mullins ss. ,per the nurse 9s. 3d. The nurses' report was presented, in which she stated that she had attended 35 cases, making to them a total number of visits of 540,, during the ten weeks she had been in the district. To one case she had to make 101 visits, to another 69 visits, and 53 and 47 visits respectively to two others. The report was ordered to be filed, and the Secretary was instructed to acknowledge its receipt, and to express the general satisfaction of the Committee at the way in which Miss Wilson had carried out her duties.— The meeting was then adjourned. At the adjourned meeting held on Tuesday, the following were present, Revs. J. Carson, J. Allatt, F. J. Lennon, E. W. W. Kaye, Drs. Mouncey and Valentine, Mr. Dring and the Secre- tary. The Rev. J. Carson presided. Letters of apology were read from Revs. H. Monk and T. Wynne-Jones,Dr. Patterson and Mr. J. E. Worsley. The committee discussed the small amount received as donations by the nurse, during the ten weeks she had been in the district, and it was considered that more stress should be laid on this matter, and recomnaendors were desired to make a point of suggesting to patients the desirability of donations being made to assist the work. The Secretary reported that a suggestion had been conveyed to him for holding a Cycle Lantern Parade,in aid of tho Society, during the autumn, and the Committee I gave him full power to act as circumstances arose. Mr. Kirk of Stirling and Co. ,presented two bed pans to ' the Society, which the Committee gratefully acknow- legged. A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the pro- ceedings.

Runcornians have indeed good reason to feel proud in the possession of a Tonic Sol-fa phoir. To win such laurels as our local choristers have done recently not only requires the utmost dilig- ence in the study of their task, but also excep- tional talent to begin with. Now that the choir have once more shown their worth, and that in the presence of masters holding the most prominent .positions in the musical world, both admiration and spontaneous assistance ought surely to be forthcom- ing in thA near future in order that these additional expenses, in the search for fame, might not be too keenly felt.

, , An incident which occurred within the la,t few day lie. for special comment in this column. The reason for so doing will only too forcibly be realized when thc safety of the public is taken into consider- ation, The incident was that qf the narrow escape from being shot experienced by Dr. MucLenns.n of Runcorn as he was driving to Weston. The doctor heard the report of firearms and immediately i felt that he had been grazed on the right hand by some small hard missiles. i The occurrence is of a most serious nature, and had the medical gentleman not had a very pressing case 1 attendlo, he would have enquired into the cir- t'• nstances. However, it is to be hoped that the el-11. .9 which has been published of it will have a not*. effect upon those wh,s use such dangerous P'°l er to be very cautious in future in which weaporm 'hey fire when near to public highways. direction 1. precaution is used we may expect at Unless moil accident of a most serious nature, any time sno • y possibly result in the loss of and which ma. human life. ---

It is rather opportune at the present time pass a few remarks with reference to tie Chiefeonsk able of Cheshire's quarterly return of drunkenness. In another column it will be seen that, whilst llyk 'e has the highest number of cases of drunkennest. • Runcorn holds the enviable reputation of possesa-' ing the lowest. The figures were submittet, at the last meeting of the Cheshire Standing Joint Cora- . rnittee and many congratulatory remarks concern- ing Runcorn were passed. Our local Councillor, Mr. Phillip Speakman, described us as "a model , town," and there is a great deal of truth in that statement. This news must certainly appear very gratifying to our temperance organization, but let us express a hope that the efforts of the members of that body will in no way be relaxed as a result, but rather cn the contrary be redoubled until drunken- ness is brought to a minimum.

The annual report of the Runcorn Free Library Committee is on the whole very pleasing. By many individuals, who take an interest in the beneficial work of the Library, it was feared that the decrease in the issue of boc.ks would this year be much greater thEn it really was, in view of the largely diminished population, following on the comp:e.tion of thp Ship Canal In reality, however, there may be said to be an increase in the aggregate number issued, because it has not decreased in proportion with the large number of mechanics who have left the town.

div.head: PHARMACY ACT AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE PHARMACY ACT AT ST. HELENS.

ALLEGED ILLEGAL SALE OF POISONS. At the St. Helens County Court, on WednesdaY. before Judge Shand, a case was heard in which the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain claimed a penalty of -£5 from J. Ernest Edington, of 135 Westfield-st. Helens, an assistant at the World's Drug Stores, for committing a breach of the Pharmacy Act, 1868, by selling poison, defendant not being duly qualified. The plaintiff was Richard Bembridge, regis" trar of the Pharmaceutical Society, represented by Mr. ' T.R. Grav,barrister (instructed by Messrs.l4lux,Thonap- son, and -Flux, London); and Mr.H. L. Riley, St.Heleo9, defended.—Mr. Gray said defendant carried on business., at 135, Westfield-st., and the claim was in respect of the sale of a bottle of Dr. Collis Brown's chlorodyne. That contained about three-quarters or more of a grain of morphine,which was a poison under the schedule of the Pharmacy Act, 1868: The action was taken under 31 and 32 Victoria. chapter 121, section 15, under which any unqualified person came who sold any of the sons specified in the Act, except under the actual, personal superintendence of a registered chemist.— For the defence, Mr. Riley said the defendant was the son of a gentleman formerly in business in St. Flelen6l- - had had large experience. He was the assistant of Mr. Peter Webster Harrison, a qualified man, and defendant would swear that on this occasion, when be sold the chlorodyne to Fouldes, Mr. flarrison was in an inner room, and that he first went to him with the bottle before selling it. Even if his Honour did think technical effence had been committed, he (Nlr. Riley) submitted that it was of so trivial a nature thst he might exercise the power conferred on County Court" judges and dismiss it.—After further evidence had been given His ffonour said he was not going to convict unless there was abundant evidence, and he was not satisfied that the Act had been transgressed. The eag°' was practically a criminal one, and it was perfectls, riglit that everybody that transgressed the Act should be punished, and punished severely, but before they were punished the offence most be made out.—Judgmentl' was given for the defendant with costs.
